# Methodological Tensions in Difference-in-Differences Following the Staggered Adoption Critique: A Critical Synthesis of New Estimators and Their Adoption in Top Economics Journals (2020–2024)

## 1. The "Goodman-Bacon (2021) Critique" and the Breakdown of TWFE

Andrew Goodman-Bacon's decomposition theorem [Journal of Econometrics, 225(2), 2021] demonstrated that the canonical two-way fixed effects (TWFE) DiD coefficient equals a weighted average of all possible 2×2 group/time DiD estimators in the data. Three distinct comparison types emerge: (i) treated vs. never-treated, (ii) earlier-treated vs. later-treated (using the later-treated group as a pre-treatment control), and (iii) later-treated vs. earlier-treated (using the already-treated group as a control — the so-called "forbidden comparison"). Weights are proportional to timing-group sizes and to the variance of the treatment dummy in each pair, with the largest weights typically accruing to mid-panel adopters [Goodman-Bacon 2021, *J. Econometrics*; decomposition command documented at https://diff-diff.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api/bacon.html].

The consequence of Theorem 1 is sharp: causal interpretation of TWFE under staggered adoption requires both parallel trends *and* treatment effects constant over time. When treatment effects differ across cohorts or evolve with exposure, TWFE estimands can have negative weights — so the regression coefficient can be negative when all cohort-time ATTs are positive [de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille, *AER* 110(9), 2020, https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20181169]. Empirically, in 200 replicated published staggered DiD studies, TWFE point estimates differ from Callaway–Sant'Anna by more than 20% in 38% of studies, with sign disagreements in 7% [Difference-in-Differences with Staggered Adoption: Bias Magnitude in 200 Published Studies, clawRxiv 2604.00789]. The magnitude of TWFE bias correlates r = 0.72 with treatment-effect heterogeneity across cohorts and r = 0.58 with the number of timing groups; studies with ≤3 timing groups exhibit mean |TWFE–CS|/|CS| of just 8%, while those with >10 groups show mean bias of 34%.

## 2. Three Methodological Responses: Family Resemblances and Divergences

The post-2021 literature developed three main families of estimators that all "isolate clean comparisons and aggregate them with user-specified weights" [Roth, Sant'Anna, Bilinski, Poe (RSBP), *J. Econometrics* 235:2218–2244, 2023, https://psantanna.com/files/RSBP_DiD_Review.pdf]. They differ in what counts as a "clean" comparison, how the baseline period is chosen, and which parallel-trends generalization they invoke.

### 2.1 Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) – Two-Stage Group-Time ATTs

Callaway and Sant'Anna (*J. Econometrics* 225(2):200–230, https://psantanna.com/files/Callaway_SantAnna_2020.pdf) define the group-time average treatment effect ATT(g,t) = E[Y_t(g) − Y_t(0) | G_g = 1] for each cohort g at calendar time t. Identification follows from a "no selection after conditioning" parallel trends assumption — either unconditional or conditional on covariates. Three estimation routes are available: outcome regression, inverse probability weighting, and a doubly-robust (DR) AIPW estimator; the paper also establishes the validity of a multiplier bootstrap that delivers *simultaneous* (rather than pointwise) confidence bands for the entire dynamic path [https://bcallaway11.github.io/did/articles/did-basics.html].

Aggregation proceeds in a second stage at the researcher's discretion: "simple" weights by cohort share, "cohort," "calendar," or event-study aggregations over event-time e = t − g. The comparison group can be either never-treated units or (when no such group exists) not-yet-treated units. Crucially, the baseline period is the single last pre-treatment period (g − 1) for each cohort; multiple pre-periods are not pooled into the counterfactual.

### 2.2 Sun and Abraham (2021) – Interaction-Weighted Estimator

Sun and Abraham (*J. Econometrics* 225(2):175–199, https://lsun20.github.io/event_studies_paper.pdf) propose an interaction-weighted (IW) estimator built on a saturated TWFE regression of Y on cohort × relative-time dummies:

Y_{i,t} = α_i + λ_t + Σ_g Σ_e [δ_{g,e} · 1{G_i = g} · D^e_{i,t}] + ε_{i,t}

The cohort-share weights Pr{E_i = e | E_i ∈ [−e, T−e]} are computed from sample proportions; IW then re-aggregates cohort-specific CATT(e,ℓ) estimates using these shares. The method is implemented via `fixest::feols(y ~ sunab(cohort, time) | unit + time)` in R or `eventstudyinteract` in Stata [https://ideas.repec.org/c/boc/bocode/s458978.html]. Compared to CS, Sun–Abraham uses a regression-based (saturated) platform that permits easy integration into standard TWFE workflows; on the other hand, Callaway–Sant'Anna's 2×2 panel approach yields a more transparent decomposition and bootstrap-based simultaneous inference.

### 2.3 Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024) – The Imputation Estimator

Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (BJS, *Rev. Econ. Studies* 91(6):3253–3285, 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12419) take a fundamentally different tack. Rather than building group-time 2×2 cells, BJS estimates unit + time fixed effects on the *untreated* sample (never-treated plus not-yet-treated observations of eventually-treated units), imputes the counterfactual Y(0) for every treated observation, and computes τ̂_{i,t} = Y_{i,t} − Ŷ_{i,t}(0); these are then aggregated to a target parameter using researcher-chosen weights. Inference uses a clustered bootstrap of residuals; the estimator is semiparametrically *efficient* for the average treatment effect on the treated under parallel trends — no other parallel-trends-respecting estimator of the same target can have smaller asymptotic variance.

In simulations and in their tax-rebate application, BJS confidence intervals are approximately 50% shorter than Callaway–Sant'Anna's and roughly 2–3.5× shorter than Sun–Abraham's when effects are plausibly homogeneous across cohorts; efficiency gains of 20–40% over equal-weighted cohort estimators are typical [https://diff-diff.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/imputation.html; https://www.causalreview.com/articles/the-borusyak-jaravel-spiess-imputation-estimator-efficient-did-for-staggered-adoption-settings]. When effects are heterogeneous, BJS retains consistency but loses its efficiency edge; the point estimates are nevertheless numerically equivalent to those of Gardner (2021) and the two-stage Wooldridge (2021)/did2s estimator [https://www.bu.edu/econ/files/2024/07/two-stage-differences-in-differences.pdf]. BJS's preferred baseline uses *all* pre-treatment periods (a global TWFE imputation) rather than g − 1 alone; this is more efficient when effects are constant but can accommodate longer pre-trends for testing.

### 2.4 De Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille (2020) and DID_M

The antecedent literature includes de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille (*AER* 110(9):2964–96, 2020, https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20181169), who decompose the TWFE β_fe into weights on group-time ATEs, prove those weights can be negative, and propose DID_M, which switches treatment status for one period and computes a Wald-DiD ratio on switchers. Their 2022 NBER survey (w29691; published *Econometrics Journal*) notes that 26 of the 100 most-cited AER papers from 2015–2019 estimate at least one TWFE regression [https://sciencespo.hal.science/hal-03873885v1/document].

## 3. Comparison of Performance Assumptions Across Estimators

The following table summarizes the assumptions underlying each estimator, drawn from the synthesis in RSBP (2023) and the primary papers.

| Estimator | Parallel Trends (PT) Required | Treatment-Effect (TE) Homogeneity | Anticipation / Dynamics | Comparison Group |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TWFE | Yes (canonical 2-group PT) | Yes (constant effects) | Ruled out by assumption | All others (incl. already-treated) |
| Callaway & Sant'Anna | Yes, generalized to all (g,t) pairs; can be unconditional or conditional on covariates | None — fully heterogeneous CATT(g,t) permitted | Anticipation periods can be specified; event-study aggregation allows dynamic effects | Never-treated *or* not-yet-treated |
| Sun & Abraham | Same generalized PT as CS | None — saturated CATT(g,ℓ) permitted | Same flexibility | Typically never-treated (with last-treated option) |
| Borusyak-Jaravel-Spiess | Same generalized PT on Y(0) | None for consistency; homogeneity required for efficiency gains | Multiple pre-periods allow richer dynamics; anticipation via lead periods | All untreated observations pooled |
| De Chaisemartin-D'Haultfœuille (DID_M) | PT for switchers | Restricted: instantaneous effects only | No anticipation; no dynamics in original paper | Switchers' pre-period vs. themselves |
| Roth-Sant'Anna (2023) | (Quasi-)random treatment timing; stronger identifying assumption than PT | Allows heterogeneous effects across cohorts/periods | Timing randomness subsumes anticipation | All untreated under random timing |

*Sources*: Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021); Sun and Abraham (2021); Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024); de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille (2020); Roth and Sant'Anna (*JPE: Microeconomics* 1(4):669–709, 2023, https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/726581); RSBP synthesis Table 1 (https://psantanna.com/files/RSBP_DiD_Review.pdf).

Two theoretical efficiency comparisons stand out. First, Roth and Sant'Anna (2023) show that under their design-based assumption of (quasi-)random treatment timing, the semiparametric efficiency bound for the average treatment effect (across a target class of estimands) is reached by an estimator that uses *all* untreated observations analogously to BJS, achieving standard-error reductions of 2× or more over Callaway–Sant'Anna and Sun–Abraham in applications [https://psantanna.com/files/Roth_SantAnna_Staggered.pdf]. In their police-training application, the Roth–Sant'Anna efficient estimator yields confidence intervals up to *8× shorter* than existing approaches. Second, BJS achieves a similar efficiency advantage under the weaker *parallel-trends-only* assumption by exploiting the unit+time structure of the counterfactual model; this is exactly why BJS and Roth–Sant'Anna point estimates are numerically equivalent.

## 4. Anticipation Effects and Baselines: A Subtle Practical Distinction

The estimators differ in how they treat anticipation. Callaway and Sant'Anna allow the user to set an `anticipation` parameter to ignore k periods before treatment when computing group-time ATTs; this discards information but cleanly removes anticipatory effects. Sun and Abraham and BJS both allow anticipation through lead (negative relative-time) coefficients in the saturated regression / event-study plot — including those negative-period coefficients in the pre-trend test while excluding them from the post-treatment aggregate. RSBP (2023, Section 3.4) flag that the no-anticipation assumption is often implicitly violated; under staggered adoption an event-study plot with all leads negative is consistent with anticipation.

The choice of baseline period is consequential. CS uses only the last pre-treatment period (g − 1) for each cohort; BJS uses the global pre-treatment mean (with all pre-periods), which is more efficient under homogeneity but requires no differential pre-trends between the longest-running and most recent cohorts [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11305929/]. Wooldridge's (2021) two-stage Mundlak (Muthē) approach and the did2s estimator [https://www.bu.edu/econ/files/2024/07/two-stage-differences-in-differences.pdf] numerically replicate BJS.

## 5. Adoption in AER, QJE, and JPE, 2020–2024

Direct headcounts of *AER*, *QJE*, *JPE*, *AER: Insights*, *AER: Microeconomics*, and *JPE: Microeconomics* articles are difficult because the methodology is so new. Surrogate evidence:

* The survey by Feng, Wang, and Zhou (https://personal.ntu.edu.sg/qfeng/Top%2027_20260313_FengWangZhou.pdf) finds DiD accounts for roughly 25% of microdata identification in 27 top economics journals during 2014–2018, rising to 30% in the AER specifically.

* Baker, Larcker and Wang (https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/21-112_8a5a4ab3-b9e7-447d-a0fe-a504b3890fb9.pdf) report 49% of 751 finance and accounting papers (2000–2019) use staggered DiD.

* A 2025 reproduction-piece by Baker, Callaway, Cunningham, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna [cited in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cmg777/starter-academic-v501/master/content/post/r_did2/index.md] provides a "practitioner's guide" hosted on a popular AER-author collaboration, which is itself an index of emerging best practice.

Methodological dominance in applied labor and health economics through 2024 follows a clear pattern, triangulated from (i) RSBP's checklist (which explicitly recommends the heterogeneity-robust estimators for staggered designs); (ii) Roth and Sant'Anna's resources page (https://jonathandroth.github.io/did-resources/); and (iii) the package ecosystems.

1. **Callaway–Sant'Anna is the modal workhorse.** The `did` (R) and `csdid` (Stata) packages are by far the most commonly cited. The Baker–Larcker–Wang survey finds that, among the three alternative staggered estimators (CS, SA, BJS), CS is the most adopted in finance/accounting, with Sun–Abraham second; BJS adoption lags. In labor applications, CS has become the default in policy evaluations of sick-pay mandates (Pichler and Wen, https://exa.ai/library/publication/9wq3b41rs31), noncompete agreements (https://ape.socialcatalystlab.org/papers/apep_0034/v1/paper.pdf), and the Better Work program in trade economics (Economics Letters 228, 2023).

2. **Sun–Abraham is the dominant event-study implementation.** Because it sits inside a saturated `fixest::feols` regression, Sun–Abraham's `sunab()` interacts are integrated into health economics event studies (e.g., NPCP/CHF papers that explicitly cite "Sun and Abraham (2021); Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021)").

3. **Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess is gaining rapid traction but lags in 2020–2024 published work** because the *Review of Economic Studies* publication (vol. 91(6), 2024) post-dates much of the window. The package citation count for `did_imputation` (29 citations as of 2024) and `did2s` indicates accelerating uptake in labor and macro applications.

4. **De Chaisemartin–D'Haultfœuille remains common in policy evaluation contexts** where the DID_M Wald ratio maps naturally onto an event-study design with a clean switcher subpopulation.

5. **Justification patterns:** Empirically, applied authors in top journals rarely run their own Monte Carlo simulations to choose among estimators; instead, justification typically cites (a) RSBP's checklist, (b) the original methodological papers for theoretical guarantees, (c) replication of canonical applications like Callaway–Sant'Anna's minimum-wage example. Sensitivity analyses follow recommended templates: Callaway–Sant'Anna event-study plots with joint Wald pre-trend tests (event_plot) and HonestDiD/Mbar robustness checks alongside point estimates. The Rambachan–Roth (2023) *RES* "A More Credible Approach to Parallel Trends" has been adopted as the sensitivity-analysis standard, with the HonestDiD package as the implementation [https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/HonestDiD/refman/HonestDiD.html].

## 6. How the New Estimators Address Roth (2022) Pre-Trend Concerns

Jonathan Roth's "Pretest with Caution" (*AER: Insights* 4(3):305–322, 2022, https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aeri.20210236) documented two problems with the standard pre-trends test: (a) conventional pre-tests are typically *underpowered* in the published economics literature (his survey of 70 AER/QJE/JPE papers with event-study plots found that the median power against violations producing effect-sized biases is low); and (b) *conditioning on passing* a pre-test introduces pre-test bias — in non-pathological cases, the conditional bias is *worse* than the unconditional bias. His simulations, calibrated to real published papers, demonstrate non-trivial coverage distortions.

The staggered DiD estimators respond to Roth's critique in three complementary ways:

### 6.1 Joint Pre-Trend Tests with Power Diagnostics

Callaway and Sant'Anna's `did` package implements a pre-test on *all* pre-treatment group-time cells jointly, returning a Wald statistic with a multiplicity correction. Crucially, RSBP (2023) recommend "accompanying the event-study plot with diagnostics of the power of the pre-test against relevant alternatives and/or non-inferiority tests" (Table 1 of RSBP). Roth's `pretrends` R package (https://github.com/jonathandroth/pretrends) computes the *minimum detectable violation* (MDV) for a given power — analogous to the MDE concept in RCT power analysis — so that a researcher can quantify what the pre-test *could* have detected. A pre-test that only has power against violations that are implausibly large is uninformative; this reframing directly responds to Roth (2022)'s under-power finding.

### 6.2 Event-Study Aggregation Removes Pre-Testing Distortion

Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024) explicitly develop a pre-test that does not contaminate the estimate. They propose a placebo test in which the imputation model is fit on the *post*-treatment observations of untreated units and the imputed versus actual pre-period values are compared; the estimator of treatment effects is then computed *unconditionally* — without conditioning on the pre-test result — using a conservative clustered variance estimator (Theorem 3). This procedure decouples pre-trend validation from inference on the treatment effect, thereby sidestepping Roth (2022)'s pre-test bias.

### 6.3 Sensitivity Analysis via Rambachan and Roth (2023)

The strongest formal response to Roth (2022) is Rambachan and Roth (2023), "A More Credible Approach to Parallel Trends" (*RES* 90(5):2555–2591, https://www.restud.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/MS30764manuscript.pdf). Rather than *testing* pre-trends, they construct confidence sets that are uniformly valid under restrictions on the post-treatment violation of parallel trends. Restrictions take two forms: (i) the post-period violation is bounded in magnitude by $\bar{M}$ times the largest pre-period violation (the "smoothness" restriction, $\Delta^{RM}$); or (ii) the post-period violation evolves smoothly through second differences ($\Delta^{SD}$). The corresponding R/Stata package is `HonestDiD`.

The recent applied DiD workflow that has emerged from this literature — illustrated in the labor/health replications of the Medicaid expansion literature (Rios-Avila, Sant'Anna and Callaway 2022; Connolly et al. 2022, https://strathprints.strath.ac.uk/91301/) — now routinely reports: (i) TWFE alongside Callaway–Sant'Anna; (ii) a joint Wald pre-trend test for the CS estimator; (iii) Sun–Abraham IW event-study coefficients as a robustness check; and (iv) an HonestDiD M-bar breakdown value stating how large a parallel-trends violation would need to be to overturn the conclusion. This multi-estimator-with-sensitivity approach has become the de facto standard for staggered DiD in labor and health economics.

## 7. Conclusion: Where the Field Stands

Across all three estimator families — Callaway–Sant'Anna, Sun–Abraham, and Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess — there is conceptual unification: decompose staggered DiD into clean 2×2 or cohort-time cells, aggregate with transparent, policy-relevant weights. The differences are largely about efficiency (BJS most efficient, CS less efficient, SA least efficient), implementation friction (CS the most modular, SA the most regression-friendly, BJS the most powerful under homogeneity), and inference style (CS delivers simultaneous bands via the multiplier bootstrap, SA and BJS use cluster-robust or residual bootstrap).

For applied labor and health economics in *AER*, *QJE*, and *JPE* during 2020–2024, Callaway–Sant'Anna has achieved *methodological dominance* — appearing not as a single paper but as a *checklist* embedded in RSBP, in the Roth–Sant'Anna efficient-estimator paper, and in Baker–Callaway–Cunningham–Goodman-Bacon–Sant'Anna's forthcoming practitioner's guide. Sun–Abraham follows closely behind for event-study reporting. The newer Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess imputation estimator is ascendant for cases where homogeneity is plausible and statistical power is paramount, but the *RES* publication date (2024) means its dominant 2020–2024 footprint lies in NBER and working-paper form.

Justification in applied work overwhelmingly relies on theoretical guarantees cited from the original papers plus sensitivity analysis à la Rambachan–Roth; only a minority of papers conduct their own Monte Carlo simulations to motivate the choice. Pre-trends are no longer tested in isolation: the convention is now a joint test plus HonestDiD sensitivity with M-bar reporting — Roth (2022)'s critique has, in practice, reshaped the evidentiary standard applied to staggered DiD in the very journals where the methodological debate began.

---

# CNC Selection for Titanium Aerospace Machining in Northern Mexico
## DMG MORI NLX 2500SY vs. Mazak Integrex i-400S vs. Okuma Multus U4000

---

## Critical clarification: the 15,000-hour utilization figure

A single calendar year contains 8,760 hours (24 h × 365 days). 15,000 annual hours therefore cannot be the workload of one machine — it exceeds physical time. Realistic interpretations:

- **Fleet total:** 15,000 hr/yr spread across multiple machines (e.g., 6 machines × ~2,500 hr each).
- **Lifecycle target:** ~15,000 cumulative cutting hours over a 6–7-year machine life, equating to ~2,200–2,500 spindle hours per year — typical of 2-shift aerospace production.
- **CAPA error:** Some shops quote "machine hours" including unmanned warm-up, tool change and idle states, inflating true spindle hours by 30–50%.

For single-shift budgeting assume **2,000–2,500 spindle-hr/yr/machine**; for 2-shift lights-out **4,000–4,500 hr/yr/machine**. Anything beyond 6,000 hr/yr on a single machine is considered "extreme duty" and accelerates spindle wear dramatically. The DMG MORI "MASTER spindles with 36-month warranty and unlimited spindle hours" benefit ([dmgmori.com](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500-2nd)) is uniquely valuable under such duty cycles. Plan your 15,000 hr/yr shop floor accordingly — the choice below must be made *per machine*, then sized to fleet.

---

## 1. Spindle torque & rigidity

| Specification | DMG MORI NLX 2500SY | Mazak Integrex i-400S | Okuma Multus U4000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main spindle power (cont.) | 26 kW @ 4,000 rpm (high-output) | 30 kW @ 3,300 rpm | 22 kW cont. (32 kW @ 30 min, high-torque opt.) |
| Main spindle torque | **828 Nm (10")**, **1,273 Nm (12")** | **1,400 Nm (≈1,032 ft-lbs)** | 477 Nm cont., **700 Nm (30 min)**, 955 Nm with high-torque option |
| Counter/sub spindle | 11 kW @ 6,000 rpm (Gen1); up to 10" / 577 Nm @ 5,000 rpm (Gen2) | 26 kW @ 4,000 rpm, 8" chuck (sub, torque ~500 Nm) | 22/15 kW @ 4,000 rpm, ~287–420 Nm |
| Milling spindle | BMT60, 12,000 rpm, 86–100 Nm | Capto C6, 12,000 rpm (20,000 rpm opt.), 22 kW, **120 Nm** | Capto C6 H1, 12,000 rpm, 30 HP intermittent |
| Y-axis | ±50 mm (Gen1) / ±60 mm (Gen2) | ±130 mm (260 mm total) | ±150 mm (300 mm total) |
| Weight | 6,400 kg | **16,200 kg** | ~14,000 kg |
| Chuck | 10" A2-8 (12" optional) | 10" A2-8 main, 8" A2-8 sub | 8–10" A2-8 standard, A2-11 optional |
| Rigid guideway | Slideways X/Y/Z + 55 mm roller guides | Linear roller | Linear roller (X,Y,Z) |

Sources: [DMG MORI NLX 2500 product page](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500-2nd); [Mazak Integrex i-400S listing, Törner](https://cnc-toerner.de/pt/maschine/mazak-integrex-i-400-s-18/); [Okuma MULTUS U series brochure Jun 2025](https://www.okuma.com/files/documents/MULTUS-U-Series_Jun2025-P500.pdf).

**For Ti-6Al-4V aerospace milling on long-reach tooling:** the Mazak Integrex i-400S has the largest torque envelope on the main turning spindle (~1,400 Nm) and the most powerful dedicated milling spindle (120 Nm, 22 kW). The Okuma U4000's high-torque option (955 Nm) is the only mill-turn competitor offering a torque curve that approaches Mazak's. The DMG MORI NLX 2500SY is fundamentally a turning-mill (not a full multi-tasking centre) with comparatively modest milling torque (≤100 Nm), making it best for chucked titanium shafts and flange turning rather than complex prismatic milling.

---

## 2. Rigidity for titanium

- **DMG MORI**: FEM-analyzed high-rigidity bed, **"30 % higher rigidity than previous series"** with 50 %-more-rigid ball-screw drives via enlarged bearings; ribbed castings ([be.dmgmori.com, NLX Innovation Days 2016](https://be.dmgmori.com/news-and-media/news/chicago-innovation-days-2016-nlx-2500sy-700)).
- **Mazak Integrex**: 16,200 kg mass and orthogonal bed design provide the highest static stiffness-to-mass of the three, important for chatter-prone Ti-6Al-4V milling.
- **Okuma Multus U4000**: **diagonal-rib bed castings** giving "7× the rigidity" vs non-ribbed structure; orthogonal 3-axis column feed with roller bearings — engineered specifically for stable 5-axis machining ([Okuma brochure](https://www.okuma.com/files/documents/MULTUS-U-Series_Jun2025-P500.pdf)).

For chatter-resistant titanium milling with extended tools, Okuma and DMG MORI both publish explicit rigidity claims supported by machine mass data; Mazak's published posture is mass-based and supported by an extensive Aerospace Center of Excellence heritage ([Mazak aerospace](https://www.mazak.com/jp-en/products/aerospace/)).

---

## 3. Recommended tooling — ceramic limitations for titanium

The peer-reviewed evidence is unambiguous: **alumina- and SiC-whisker-reinforced ceramic tools are unsuitable for Ti-6Al-4V**, even at low cutting speeds and even with high-pressure coolant. Failure modes are chemical reactivity with titanium, chipping/fracture of the edge, accelerated crater wear, and surface roughness above aerospace limits (5.5 µm measured vs 1.6 µm rejection criteria).

> "Silicon carbide whisker reinforced (WG 300 grade) alumina ceramic tools are not suitable for machining titanium alloys, even when using other cutting environments, due to the accelerated tool wear and chipping/fracture of the cutting edge associated with chemical interactions between the ceramic tools and titanium alloys." — [Academia.edu / Comparative Analysis of SiAlON, CBN & Carbide for Ti (2024)](https://www.academia.edu/114605495/Comparative_Analysis_of_the_Cutting_Performances_of_SiAlON_Ceramic_Cubic_Boron_Nitride_and_Carbide_Cutting_Tools_for_Titanium_Machining)

> "Conventional micron-grain size ceramic tools have not proved better when machining titanium… due to the chemical interactions between the ceramic tools and titanium alloys" — [ABCM COBEM 2007 evaluation of nano-grain ceramics on Ti-6Al-4V](https://abcm.org.br/anais/cobem/2007/pdf/COBEM2007-0854.pdf)

> "SiAlON ceramic cutting inserts… flake/wear mechanism at higher speeds in dry machining… lower cutting force (beyond v = 80 m/min) than ceramic insert due to its better thermo-chemical stability." — [Sadhana/IASc 2022](https://www.ias.ac.in/article/fulltext/sadh/047/0105) and [Springer IJA-MT 2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00170-024-13225-3).

**Practical selection rule for Ti-6Al-4V on these three machines:**

| Class | Suitability | Application |
|---|---|---|
| **Uncoated / TiN-coated carbide** | Avoid | Severe chemical affinity, dissolution wear |
| **AlTiN-coated carbide end mills** | **Recommended** | Maximum tool life for micro & profile milling ([PMC/NIH, Cutting Performance of Coated Micro End Mills in Ti-6Al-4V](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6267563/)) |
| **AlCrN-coated carbide** | Strong alternative | Good for chipping-resistance |
| **PCD (polycrystalline diamond)** | Best tool life at low speeds | Limited to non-ferrous; only viable for finish operations on titanium if Ti content of compound is low (rare) |
| **SiAlON ceramic inserts** | Marginal | May be viable under **high-pressure coolant** at moderate speeds (<200 m/min) — but with elevated fracture risk |
| **Al₂O₃ / SiC-whisker ceramic** | **Do not use** | Documented chemical reactivity, fracture |
| **CBN** | Not generally recommended for Ti | Reactivity and rapid wear |

Through-cryogenic / high-pressure (≥70 bar) coolant is the single biggest productivity lever in Ti-6Al-4V — all three machines support high-pressure coolant options, but the value depends on shop plumbing, not the machine.

---

## 4. Thermal compensation for ±0.0005" tolerance (±12.7 µm)

±0.0005" is an aggressive, single-part tolerance and is at the outer edge of what any of these machines can hold *without active thermal compensation*. Here is each machine's published thermal-stability data:

**DMG MORI NLX 2500 / 2nd Gen**
- Coolant circulation through castings, ball-screw core cooling, spindle oil jacket around motor unit.
- Internal data: **thermal displacement 2.0 µm at 3,200 rpm under constant ambient** ([Tuyap NLX 2500 brochure](https://docs.tuyap.online/FDOCS/95474.pdf)).
- NLX 2500|1250 2nd Gen reduces internal/external temperature effects "and keeps radial displacement within **7 µm even during continuous operation**" with Magnescale MAP offset ([Marketscreener / DMG MORI Sep 2025](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/dmg-mori-launch-of-the-nlx-2500-1250-2nd-generation-br-realize-mx-with-process-integration-aut-ce7d58dfd880f72c)).
- C-axis index: 0.001° (guaranteed 0.003°).

**Mazak Integrex i-400S** (SmoothAi-era features)
- Ai Thermal Shield: learns from accumulated data; **cutting-edge position correction as a function of spindle speed, ambient temp, machine position and coolant state** ([Mazak INTEGREX i NEO Thermal Shield](https://www.mazak.com/us-en/products/integrex-i-neo/)).
- Standard: spindle temperature-controlled oil jacket + X/Y/Z ball-screw core cooling.
- Quantitative data not published for the i-400S specifically — the Ai system relies on learning-cycle tuning. Holding ±12.7 µm requires a thermal-stabilized environment, warm-up cycle and **typically ambient controlled to ±1 °C**.

**Okuma Multus U4000**
- Thermo-Friendly Concept with **TAS-C (Construction)** and **TAS-S (Spindle)** active stabilization — eliminates need for warm-up and tolerates ambient shifts.
- Published: ambient change of 8 °C produces **X-axis 7 µm (∅13 µm), Y-axis 8 µm, Z-axis 9 µm** thermal displacement ([Okuma brochure](https://www.okuma.com/files/documents/MULTUS-U-Series_Jun2025-P500.pdf)).
- Suppresses **"tilt of the column and milling spindle"** even with environmental changes — directly relevant to 5-axis titanium contouring.
- 5-Axis Auto Tuning System re-measures geometric error using a datum sphere and touch probe, automatically setting compensation tables.

**Verdict on ±0.0005":** all three machines can in principle *achieve* ±12.7 µm per part but **only when** (a) shop ambient is held to ±1 °C, (b) machine warm-up cycle is observed, (c) thermal compensation is enabled and tuned. The Okuma Multus U4000 has the strongest *published* thermal compensation ("exception" performance vs "unmatched by others"), the DMG MORI NLX 2500 Gen 2 has the best *published quantification* for displacement under continuous operation (7 µm radial), and Mazak's Ai Thermal Shield is the most adaptive but is learning-cycle dependent.

---

## 5. Siemens NX CAM integration

All three are supported by Siemens NX CAM via **Post Hub / Smart Machine Kit Solutions (SMKS)** ([Siemens NX Manufacturing blog, SMKS milestone 100 kits](https://blogs.sw.siemens.com/nx-manufacturing/smart-machine-kit-solutions-hits-milestone-of-100-kits-on-siements-post-hub/); [What's new in Post Hub 2024](https://community.sw.siemens.com/s/article/What-s-new-in-Post-Hub-2024)).

| Vendor | NX CAM integration depth | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **DMG MORI** | **MTSK (Machine Tool Support Kit)** — manufacturer-certified post processor + NC simulation + virtual controller via Siemens CSE; supports **DMG MORI technology cycles** in NX simulation; in-house DMG MORI Digital development; dedicated support team. Listed as a leading Smart Machine Kit on Post Hub. | Most deeply integrated; vendor-co-developed; co-marketed by Siemens ([Siemens DMG MORI postprocessor for NX](https://www.siemens.com/en-us/products/dmg-mori-postprocessor-for-siemens-nx/); [DMG MORI Siemens NX CAD/CAM](https://us.dmgmori.com/products/digitization/work-preparation/cam-software/siemens-nx)). |
| **Mazak** | 170+ SMKS kits on Post Hub include Mazak models (e.g., Variaxis i-600, Integrex family support). Mazak also offers **MAZATROL Smooth CAM Ai** as an alternative end-to-end path with their own digital twin. | Two CAD/CAM paths available: Siemens NX with Post Hub SMKS, OR Mazak's native Smooth CAM Ai with digital twin. The latter is more tightly coupled to Mazak controls; the former is the right choice if your shop standardizes on NX. |
| **Okuma** | Postprocessor and machine model available via Post Hub; Okuma publishes its own adapter free on **OSP App Store**. OSP-P500/P500M controls run full Windows internally, so third-party postprocessors run natively. | Good but less vendor-deep than DMG MORI MTSK. Best path is OSP-P500 + THINC API + Siemens NX with Post Hub postprocessor. |

**Practical recommendation:** if your shop standardizes on **Siemens NX**, DMG MORI has the most polished, vendor-supported, end-to-end integration. Mazak and Okuma are both supported via Post Hub but Mazak's strategic push is toward Smooth CAM Ai; Okuma's strongest path is its own OSP + THINC API with Siemens NX as a complementary post-processing option.

---

## 6. AS9100D traceability via MTConnect / OPC-UA

All three machines meet the requirements — differentiators are in the *quality* and *documentation* of the data path.

**DMG MORI — Connectivity by DMG MORI**
- **IoT Connector is standard** on every new DMG MORI machine from 2020. Supports **OPC-UA, MTConnect and MQTT** simultaneously ([DMG MORI Connectivity](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/digitization/connectivity)).
- **MDC: Standardized machine data output in OPC UA, MTconnect and MQTT formats** explicitly stated ([DMG MORI NLX 2500 product page - Control & Software](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500-2nd)).
- **CELOS X Tool Master + Tool Data Exchange (TDE)** transfers tool identity via **OPC UA**, providing a per-tool, per-cutting-edge digital chain-of-custody record — directly supports AS9100D 8.5.2 (identification & traceability) ([DMG MORI Tool Master](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/digitization/celos-x/celos-x-tool-master)).
- Active in the **umati** (OPC-UA Companion Specification for machine tools) and Factory-X initiatives.

**Mazak — SmartBox 2.0 + SmoothAi**
- **All Mazak machines ship MTConnect-capable** ([Mazak USA MTConnect](https://www.mazakusa.com/machines/technology/digital-solutions/mtconnect)).
- **SmartBox 2.0 (Sep 2024)** adds **MQTT and OPC UA** protocols on top of MTConnect, with edge-compute and cybersecurity ([Mazak press release Sep 2024](https://www.mazak.com/us-en/news-media/news/mazak-advances-machine-connectivity-smart-box-2/)).
- Supports OEM-to-OEM MTConnect agents ([mtconnect.mazakcorp.com](http://mtconnect.mazakcorp.com/)).

**Okuma — OSP-P500 + Connect Plan**
- **Okuma MTConnect agent available free via the OSP App Store** — built on a full Windows control, no external box needed ([Okuma MTConnect](https://www.okuma.com/mtconnect); [ThingConnect integration guide](https://thingconnect.io/integrations/machine-brands/okuma)).
- **OSP-P500M and OSP-P700A add a factory-installed OPC-UA server** built to the OPC Foundation CNC information model (same standard as umati).
- **Connect Plan** factory-monitoring suite with archival data for AS9100D §7.5.3 (records) and §8.5 (production).
- OPC-UA communication encryption per Okuma P500 cyber-security release ([Okuma Press Release Jun 2023](https://www.okuma.eu/newsroom/press-releases/detail/next-generation-cnc-control/)).

For AS9100D, all three deliver compliant data; the **DMG MORI** stack has the most formalized tool-data lineage (TDE via OPC-UA scans), the **Mazak** stack has the strongest cybersecurity posture (SmartBox 2.0), and the **Okuma** stack is the most open/flexible (Windows-based OSP, App Store model) with the most distributed factory-monitoring ecosystem across all skill levels.

---

## 7. Nuevo León service infrastructure

All three OEMs maintain their principal service presence in the **Monterrey / Apodaca aerospace cluster**, which is a major reason to site aerospace work in Nuevo León:

**DMG MORI México S.A. de C.V.**
- Address: **Citio Torre Aeropuerto, Av. Miguel Alemán 248, Piso 5, Zona Centro, C.P. 66600 Apodaca, Nuevo León** ([mx.dmgmori.com locations](https://mx.dmgmori.com/empresa/ubicaciones/dmg-mori-mexico)).
- National parts warehouse ("Centro Nacional de Refacciones") in **Querétaro, Parque Industrial Benito Juárez** — 13× expansion to 490 m² ([Mexicoindustry 2018](https://mexicoindustry.com/index.php/noticia/establecen-en-quertaro-su-centro-nacional-de-refacciones)).
- Dedicated **Aerospace Center of Excellence** ([mx.dmgmori.com aerospace](https://mx.dmgmori.com/soluciones/focus-industries/aviation-space)).
- Service hotline: 01-800 DMG MORI.

**Mazak Mexico S.A. de C.V. (Mexico Technology Center)**
- **Spectrum 100, Parque Industrial Finsa, Apodaca, Nuevo León 66600** ([Mazak US-es Nuevo Leon](https://www.mazak.com/us-es/about-us/mazak-representative/nuevo-leon/); [Mazak Mexico Technology Center](https://www.mazak.com/us-en/about-us/support-bases0/Mexico_Technology_Center/)).
- **One of 8 Technology Centers in North America**.
- After-hours service: **1-800-231-1456**.
- Regional Service Manager: Gustavo Alarcón.
- Free Mazatrol programming training for 3 years post-purchase at the Mexico Technology Center.
- Independent authorized dealer **Pypesa-Mazak (Guadalajara)** supports the western region ([pypesamaquinariacnc.com](https://pypesamaquinariacnc.com/maquinas-y-servicios/)).

**Okuma Mexico Tech Center at HEMAQ Monterrey**
- **25,000 ft², Monterrey, "industrial capital of Mexico"** ([Okuma Monterrey tech center](https://www.okuma.com/okuma-tech-centers/monterrey)).
- **HEMAQ Monterrey is the exclusive Okuma distributor in Mexico since 1989** with **4,000+ machines installed** ([Okuma Press Release Mar 2013](https://www.okuma.com/es-mx/press/okuma-opens-new-tech-center-in-mexico)).
- Address: J. Cantu Garcia 601, Col. Garza Cantu, San Nicolas de los Garza, N.L. 66480; Corporate +52-81-8131-3199.
- **AS9100 Rev. D certified at CentroTec Monterrey** (a differentiator — your AS9100D QMS can directly inherit these processes) ([HEMAQ AS9100](https://www.hemaq.com/venta-maquinas-herramienta-cnc/)).
- 24/7/365 service via 877-700-5060 toll-free US line; WhatsApp +52 (81) 1910 3199.

**Cluster-level observation:** all three OEMs are physically present within 25 km of each other in the Apodaca/Monterrey aerospace corridor, giving the shop geographic redundancy. Mazak and DMG MORI are most concentrated near the airport (Apodaca), while Okuma/HEMAQ is in nearby San Nicolás de los Garza. **Okuma has the only AS9100D-certification explicitly published for its Monterrey tech center** — relevant for AS9100D audit evidence.

---

## 8. Long-term operating cost drivers

In rough order of cost-weight for an aerospace shop running Ti-6Al-4V:

| Driver | DMG MORI NLX 2500SY | Mazak Integrex i-400S | Okuma Multus U4000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Spindle replacement (typical 1×/4-7 yr at high duty)** | TurnMASTER, **36-month unlimited-hours warranty** ([DMG MORI Gen 2](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500-2nd)) | Standard OEM warranty | Standard OEM warranty |
| **Tooling consumption** (largest variable) — driven by thermal stability & rigidity | High rigidity; thermal stability helps | Highest mass, best for chatter resistance | High rigidity, Thermo-Friendly stability |
| **Coolant & consumables** | zero-sludgeCOOLANT pro (option), energy savings 16 % via GREENMODE ([DMG MORI Gen 2](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500-2nd)) | SmartBox analytics for coolant life monitoring | ECO suite plus standard on P500 ([Okuma OSP-P500 page](https://www.okuma.com/cnc-osp-p500)) |
| **Energy consumption** | 16 % less energy, GREENMODE options | Comparable class | ECO Idling Stop, ECO Operation, ECO Power Monitor |
| **Service contract / response time** | Apodaca NL, Querétaro parts | Apodaca NL Tech Center, 24/7 US hotline | HEMAQ Monterrey 24/7/365 US toll-free; AS9100D certified |
| **Connectivity / data infrastructure** | IoT Connector included, CELOS X included | SmartBox 2.0 sold as accessory | MTConnect adapter free; OPC UA on P500M/P700A |
| **CAM / postprocessor licensing** | MTSK tightly integrated with NX; OSP/MAPPS also supported | Mazak Smooth CAM Ai free for buyers; NX CAM via Post Hub | Free MTConnect adapter; NX CAM via Post Hub |
| **Spindle obsolescence** | MASTER turnMASTER generation, common across NLX line | Long-running Integrex platform, mature spare-parts logistics | Single-source manufacture (Okuma makes its own motors/encoders/spindles/controls) |
| **Automation retrofit cost** | Robo2Go Turning / AMR 1000 plug&play | PLUG-IN Pallet Cell, SmartBox | Robo2Go via DMG MORI is not relevant here; Okuma offers its own automation cell options |
| **Floor space / kg-per-m²** | 6.4 t — densest | 16.2 t — largest footprint | ~14 t class |

**Single biggest controllable cost:** **tooling consumption in Ti-6Al-4V.** The trio that minimizes tool-change cycle time, machined-in-process measurement (eliminating scrap parts) and has the most stable thermal control will produce the lowest per-part cost. The DMG MORI's MASTER spindle warranty (unlimited hours for 36 months) directly reduces a major risk cost. Okuma's "single-source manufacturer of mechanics, electronics, IT and controls" reduces long-term obsolescence risk — Okuma makes its own motors, encoders, spindles and CNC, which protects against catastrophic part-availability surprises 10+ years out.

---

## 9. Composite recommendation matrix

Use this to score for the specific job mix in your Nuevo León shop:

| Decision factor | DMG MORI NLX 2500SY | Mazak Integrex i-400S | Okuma Multus U4000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Heavy chucked Ti shaft turning | ★★★★★ (1,273 Nm opt.) | ★★★★★ (1,400 Nm) | ★★★★☆ (955 Nm opt.) |
| Complex 5-axis prismatic Ti parts | ★★★☆☆ (mill-turn) | ★★★★★ (B-axis, full 5-axis multitasks) | ★★★★★ (B-axis + lower turret option) |
| Tight ±0.0005" tolerance | ★★★★☆ (7 µm radial documented) | ★★★★☆ (Ai learning; spec not published) | ★★★★★ (8 µm Y over 8 °C ambient documented) |
| Siemens NX CAM integration depth | ★★★★★ (vendor-cert MTSK) | ★★★★☆ (Post Hub SMKS) | ★★★★☆ (Post Hub + THINC API) |
| AS9100D data traceability | ★★★★★ (TDE tool lineage via OPC-UA) | ★★★★☆ (SmartBox 2.0 MTConnect+OPCUA) | ★★★★☆ (Connect Plan, MTConnect, OPC UA) |
| Nuevo León service proximity | ★★★★☆ (Apodaca) | ★★★★★ (Apodaca NL Tech Center) | ★★★★★ (Monterrey + AS9100D cert) |
| Spindle warranty advantage | ★★★★★ (36 mo unlimited) | ★★★☆☆ | ★★★☆☆ |
| Tool-life stability (Ti) | ★★★★☆ | ★★★★★ (mass/rigidity) | ★★★★☆ |
| CAPEX per unit (estimated) | Mid (turning mill) | Highest (multi-tasking platform) | Mid-High |

---

## Bottom-line recommendation by use case

- **If your shop is running chucked titanium aerospace shafts, flanges and short mill-turn work**, the **DMG MORI NLX 2500SY Gen 2** is the strongest fit: best-in-class turning torque (1,273 Nm with 12" chuck), documented 7 µm continuous thermal performance, the deepest Siemens NX CAM integration (MTSK), and an unmatched 36-month unlimited-hours spindle warranty.

- **If your shop is doing complex prismatic titanium parts (structural fittings, blisks, blings, complex prismatic fittings) in one-setup DONE-IN-ONE operations**, the **Mazak Integrex i-400S** is the strongest fit: most powerful mill-turn kinematics, ~1,400 Nm turning torque, full B-axis ±130° milling, Mazak Mexico Technology Center directly in Apodaca, Mazatrol training included.

- **If your shop is doing long, slender titanium shafts with 5-axis contour features and runs hot/cold shop environments**, the **Okuma Multus U4000** is the strongest fit: diagonal-rib bed (7× rigidity claim), Thermo-Friendly Concept with published 7–10 µm stability over ±8 °C ambient swings, single-source manufacturing for low long-term obsolescence risk, HEMAQ Monterrey as an AS9100D-certified exclusive service partner, 4,000+ machines installed in Mexico since 1989.

For a **mixed-job titanium shop** running both shaft turning and 5-axis mill-turn, consider the **Okuma Multus U4000 with the high-torque spindle option** — it gives you the closest all-round package, with the strongest shop-environment tolerance and the strongest AS9100D-aligned service partner in Nuevo León.

# Real-Time Object Detection at 200×30 fps for Warehouse Inventory: YOLOv8 vs EfficientDet-D4 vs NVIDIA TAO DetectNet_v2 on Jetson AGX Orin

## Executive Summary

For a 200-camera warehouse deployment running **6,000 aggregate FPS** (33.33 ms per-frame latency budget) on Jetson AGX Orin modules with TensorRT INT8, **TAO DetectNet_v2 (ResNet-34 backbone, pruned variant)** offers the best combination of throughput-per-watt, model update infrastructure, and OTA-friendly size for a refresh-on-monthly-cadence. **YOLOv8s** is the fastest single-stream inference but has the most fragile incremental-learning pipeline. **EfficientDet-D4** is dominated on every axis relevant to this deployment. **All three frameworks achieve INT8 compression below 100 MB except YOLOv8x and DetectNet_v2 with the ResNet-34 unpruned backbone**, and INT8 accuracy floor on your custom warehouse task is realistically **mAP50-95 ~87–91%** when proper domain-matched calibration is used — below the 92% naive target.

The rest of this report substantiates each finding with measured benchmarks, sustainability/uncertainty margins, and the practical realities of edge active learning.

---

## 1. Throughput: Can Any Single AGX Orin Serve 200 Cameras at 30 fps?

**Aggregate system demand is 6,000 FPS.** No single Jetson AGX Orin — top-tier SKU with 275 Sparse INT8 TOPS — comes close.

Measured TensorRT INT8 throughput per AGX Orin 64GB at 640×640 input, batch=1, MAXN power mode (per Ultralytics' published trtexec results and EdgeAIStack benchmarks at [edgeaistack.ai/benchmarks/jetson-agx-orin](https://edgeaistack.ai/benchmarks/jetson-agx-orin/yolov8/s/)):

| Model | Engine size (INT8 TensorRT file) | FP16 FPS | INT8 FPS | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **YOLOv8n** | ~20–30 MB | ~420 | ~570 | Highest FPS, lowest accuracy |
| **YOLOv8s** | ~50 MB | 252 | 342 | Best cost/perf |
| **YOLOv8m** | ~80–120 MB | 171 | 248 | Mid-tier |
| **YOLOv8x** | ~200–300 MB | 67 | 107 | Best single-stream accuracy |
| **EfficientDet-D0** | ~14 MB | 310 | 396 | High FPS, ~34.6 COCO mAP |
| **EfficientDet-D4** | ~75 MB (weights) | est. ~25–35* | est. ~40–55* | 49.7 COCO mAP |
| **DetectNet_v2 ResNet-18 (pruned)** | ~9 MB | ~610 | ~1,116 | At 960×544, GPU BS=32 |
| **DetectNet_v2 ResNet-34 (pruned v2.3)** | ~45 MB | ~480 | 890 | At 960×544, GPU BS=32 |
| **DetectNet_v2 ResNet-34 (unpruned v2.5)** | ~85 MB | ~250 | 421 | At 960×544, GPU BS=16 |

*EfficientDet-D4 specific JetPack 6 measured numbers were not found in the corpus; on T4 TensorRT10 it is 33.55 ms per Ultralytics' comparison table, and EdgeAIStack lists EfficientDet as a family on AGX Orin 64GB at 310 fps FP16 / 395.8 fps INT8 but at 512×512 input ([edgeaistack.ai/benchmarks/jetson-agx-orin/efficientdet/d0/](https://edgeaistack.ai/benchmarks/jetson-agx-orin/efficientdet/d0/)). For 640×640 (D4's native res) the per-frame cost scales roughly 3–4× vs. D0, putting realistic INT8 throughput at **30–55 fps per stream** — well below real-time at 30 fps on a single stream once GPU sharing/NMS overhead is included.

**Capacity calculation (sustained 80% capacity, 9 AGX Orin 64GB modules per YOLOv8s):**

| Model | FPS/module | Cameras/module @ 30 fps | Modules for 200 cameras |
|---|---|---|---|
| YOLOv8s INT8 | 342 | 9.1 | 22 |
| YOLOv8m INT8 | 248 | 6.6 | 31 |
| YOLOv8x INT8 | 107 | 2.9 | 71 |
| **DetectNet_v2 ResNet-34 pruned v2.3 (BS=32)** | 890 | 23.7 | **9** |
| DetectNet_v2 ResNet-34 unpruned (BS=16) | 421 | 11.2 | 18 |
| EfficientDet-D4 INT8 (est.) | ~45 | 1.2 | 167 |

**DLA caveat.** The two DLA cores on AGX Orin run classical CNNs at lower latency-per-watt but **2–4× higher per-frame latency vs. GPU** ([ProventusNova, 2026](https://proventusnova.com/blog/tensorrt-vs-dla-jetson-orin)). DLA is the right tool for offloading a secondary worker, not for chasing the latency floor. None of the three candidate models benefits enough from DLA to change the fleet count above.

**Multi-camera vs. multi-model caveat.** The FPS figures above are **single-model shared across streams** with DeepStream's batching. Per-stream model copies drop throughput 3–8× depending on batch size and unified-memory pressure ([YOLOv8 RAM requirements on Jetson](https://edgeaistack.ai/blog/yolov8-ram-requirements-jetson/); OS baseline alone is 2.5–3.5 GB on AGX Orin 64GB). Use a **shared-model-with-batching** architecture, not per-camera models.

> **Uncertainty:** the 342/248/107 fps values are from Ultralytics' 2026 vendor benchmark on JetPack 6 + TensorRT 10.x, MAXN power mode, batch 1, single stream. Real deployments with decode + NMS + tracking typically achieve 70–85% of these numbers sustained. Plan for 22–28 AGX Orin 64GB modules for the YOLOv8s case, not the optimistic 18.

---

## 2. INT8 mAP Degradation vs. FP16 Baseline on Your Custom Set

The reliable empirical expectation for a domain-matched, well-calibrated INT8 model on a custom warehouse detection task is:

- **mAP50-95 drop of 1–3 absolute percentage points** vs. FP16 baseline, for clean conditions on medium-to-large objects
- **5–8 pp drop on small/low-contrast labels** (e.g., pallet text printed in small fonts, scuff marks on damaged corners) where box-localization sub-pixel precision matters
- **3–7 pp mAP50-95 drop observed under common PTQ when calibration data is COCO rather than your warehouse** (YOLO family, [arXiv 2508.19600](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.19600))
- **7.8 pp drop specifically for occluded targets** with naive INT8 PTQ ([MMDet-Edge, PMC12944083](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12944083/))

This implies a practical **floor of mAP50-95 ≈ 87–91%** for compressed INT8 models on warehouse data — **below the 92% naive target** unless:
1. You train **with QAT (Quantization-Aware Training)** rather than PTQ — TAO DetectNet_v2 supports this natively; YOLOv8's open-source INT8 export is PTQ-only
2. Your dataset has a balanced mix of small/damaged/large-label conditions that match your deployment distribution
3. You perform calibration on **1,000+ representative warehouse images** (the TensorRT standard rule; same images that mimic your camera angle, lighting, and SKU mix)

A specific reference point: Ultralytics' [TensorRT INT8 export PR #10165](https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/10165) achieved **mAP50-95 = 0.477** on COCO128 vs. 0.50 for FP16 YOLOv8s — a 2.3 pp loss — using dynamic shapes and TensorRT INT8.

The mAP loss is **detector-class asymmetric**:

| Detector | mAP drop FP16 → INT8 (typical) | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **YOLOv8s** (Ultralytics trtexec, Orin Nano) | 1.6 pp (44.7 → 41.2 @ INT8) but 3.5 pp for v8m | [the0807 YOLOv8-ONNX-TensorRT](https://github.com/the0807/YOLOv8-ONNX-TensorRT/) |
| **YOLOv8n** (OR T-RT, ONNX R-T CPU) | 1.5 pp (0.016 mAP on COCO val2017; small objects lose up to 5.7 pp) | [TildAlice 2026](https://tildalice.io/onnx-int8-vs-fp16-jetson-orin-nano-latency-benchmark/) |
| **EfficientDet-D4** (COCO) | n/d, but commonly 2–4 pp | qualitative Ultralytics documentation |
| **DetectNet_v2 ResNet-34 (TAO PeopleNet)** | "<1 pp typical" on TAO's published accuracy tables; QAT preserves accuracy cleanly | NGC model card & [TAO documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/tao_deploy/detectnet_v2.html) |

**DetectNet_v2 with QAT is the most INT8-friendly of the three** because TAO's quantization-aware training simulates INT8 during finetuning rather than after the fact.

---

## 3. Power Draw Under Sustained 30 fps × N-Stream Load

The AGX Orin 64GB has a 60 W module envelope (per [NVIDIA data sheet, Openzeka summary](https://openzeka.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Jetson_AGX_Orin_DS-10662-001_v1.1.pdf)); the 32 GB SKU caps at 40 W; AGX Orin Industrial at 75 W. **[NVIDIA forum-measured sustained VDD_GPU_SOC ≈ 30 W under MAXN inferencing](https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/measuring-maximum-power-consumption/319008/6)**.

Real-world measured power (single 64GB module, 1080p@30 fps, INT8+TensorRT, 72-hour burn-in, passive heatsink, 25 °C ambient — [NexusHome Intelligence, 2026](https://www.atfxcent.com/news/Edge_computing_for_smart_city__real_world_power_draw_of_NVIDIA_Jetson_AGX_Orin_in_continuous_inference.html)):

| Workload | Avg Power | Peak | Thermal Plateau |
|---|---|---|---|
| Face + License plate (2 streams) | 28.4 W | 34.1 W | 62.3 °C |
| 8-class multi-object tracking | 22.7 W | 29.8 W | 58.9 °C |
| Radar+vision fusion | 31.6 W | 37.2 W | 65.1 °C |

AgriJetsonBench on AGX Orin 64GB under matched 15 W INT8: YOLO11s reaches **80.9 FPS at 0.1814 J/inference** ([arXiv 2608.00927](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.00927)). That gives **per-frame inference energy ≈ 0.18 J on a power-capped module, and ≈ 0.06–0.10 J at full MAXN** (because inference is so much faster there). So routing some inference to DLA can lower per-frame energy, but at the cost of latency — a tradeoff appropriate only if you have a multi-worker pipeline.

**Fleet power for the 200-cam / 6,000-fps requirement:**

| Configuration | Modules | Avg fleet power | Annual energy | Annual cost @ $0.15/kWh |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| YOLOv8s @ 9 cams/mod | 22–25 | ~550–625 W | 4,800–5,500 kWh | $720–825 |
| YOLOv8m @ 6 cams/mod | 31–34 | ~775–850 W | 6,800–7,500 kWh | $1,020–1,125 |
| DetectNet_v2 v2.3 @ 23 cams/mod | **9** | ~225–270 W | **~2,000–2,400 kWh** | **$300–360** |
| EfficientDet-D4 @ ~1 cam/mod | 167 | ~4,200 W | ~37,000 kWh | $5,550 |

**DetectNet_v2 ResNet-34 pruned is a 3–5× power-and-cost advantage over YOLOv8s** for this specific fleet size, simply because you need fewer modules.

> **Uncertainty:** power figures are sensitive to cooling and power-mode selection. At MAXN Super (JetPack 6.2+, AGX Orin 32GB: 200 → 241 TOPS per [EdgeAIStack MAXN blog](https://edgeaistack.ai/blog/jetson-maxn-vs-maxn-super/)), the 64GB module can also exceed the 60 W envelope under sustained 100% GPU load, requiring active cooling in your enclosure.

---

## 4. Model-Update Pipeline: Which Framework Handles "New SKUs Monthly" Cleanly?

| Criterion | YOLOv8 (Ultralytics) | EfficientDet-D4 | **TAO DetectNet_v2** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pretrained model zoo for transfer learning | COCO only (80 classes) | COCO only | **NGC zoo (PeopleNet, TrafficCamNet, FaceDetect, etc.)** |
| First-class class-add workflow | Not built-in; "adding classes always risks forgetting" — workarounds via freezing backbone ([Ultralytics #13365](https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/issues/13365)) | No built-in workflow | **`load_graph` flag + class config in spec file** ([TAO DetectNet_v2 docs](https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/cv_finetuning/tensorflow_1/object_detection/detectnet_v2.html)) |
| Pruning + retraining | Not supported | Not supported | **Built-in: pruning → retraining → re-export** ([TAO workflow doc](https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/deprecations/tensorflow_1/object_detection/detectnet_v2.html)) |
| QAT (quantization-aware training) | Not built into Ultralytics train loop | Not available | **First-class QAT with calibration cache reuse** |
| TensorRT engine regeneration per SKU update | Manual export each time | Manual export each time | **`tao deploy detectnet_v2 gen_trt_engine` reuses spec** |
| Catastrophic-forgetting mitigation | None out-of-the-box; user must freeze backbone and replay prior classes ([Ultralytics #16283](https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/issues/16283)) | None | **Transfer learning across resolutions/domains with `load_graph=true`**, classwise cost function |
| Ecosystem for change management | Plain PyTorch checkpoints | TensorFlow saved_model (mostly archived upstream) | **TAO AutoML, Weights & Biases / ClearML integration, NGC model registry** |
| License / lifecycle signal | Active, current | **Repo effectively archived since 2021** ([Codersera](https://codersera.com/blog/efficientdet-vs-detectron2-for-object-detection-comparison/)); conversion to TensorRT is fragile | Active, NVIDIA-supported, on-prem x86 + TAO Toolkit |

**TAO DetectNet_v2 wins decisively on update pipeline robustness.** For warehouse use cases specifically, the TAO flow is the only one built for "model refinement as SKUs change" without explicit class-forgotten countermeasures. YOLOv8 can do it but requires a custom training loop with class replay plus a backbone freeze strategy (the YOLOv8 "freeze + warm-up" recipes in issues #15997 and #16283 confirm that out-of-the-box YOLOv8 will rewrite COCO classes as soon as you add a new SKU class). EfficientDet-D4 has neither the tooling nor the upstream momentum for monthly retraining.

---

## 5. Accuracy Floor When Compressing Below 100 MB for Cellular OTA

Three orthogonal compression options:
1. **Pruning** (TAO bakes this in): 2–4× size reduction with ~1 pp mAP loss recoverable via retraining
2. **INT8 quantization** (TensorRT): another 4× size reduction with the 1–3 pp drop discussed above
3. **Tensor-level delta updates** (Oxide, Mallorn, TinyMLDelta): instead of re-shipping the whole model, ship just the changed tensors — fine-tuning-only updates reduce to **KB-sized patches** ([Oxide](https://github.com/samratjha96/oxide) reports 1,263 bytes for a 2.1 MB fine-tune; TinyMLDelta 475-byte patch for 67 KB TFLite sensor model)

**Practical 100 MB compliance check for each architecture after pruning + INT8:**

| Architecture | FP16 size | Pruned + INT8 file | Under 100 MB? |
|---|---|---|---|
| YOLOv8n | 12 MB | ~3–6 MB | ✓ |
| YOLOv8s | 22 MB | ~10–21 MB | ✓ |
| **YOLOv8m** | 50 MB | ~22–45 MB | ✓ |
| YOLOv8l | 75 MB | ~34–75 MB | ✓ (borderline) |
| YOLOv8x | 130 MB | ~60–105 MB | ✗ (marginal after pruning) |
| EfficientDet-D0 | 16 MB | ~6–14 MB | ✓ |
| EfficientDet-D4 | 75 MB | ~30–75 MB | ✓ (borderline) |
| DetectNet_v2 ResNet-18 pruned | 12 MB | **~9 MB** | ✓ |
| **DetectNet_v2 ResNet-34 pruned v2.3** | 45 MB | **~30–45 MB** | ✓ |

Combined with delta encoding, monthly OTA over LTE Cat-M1/LTE-M (typical 300 kbps uplink) is fully tractable: a 30 MB update becomes **7–10 MB of delta payload for an incremental SKU add** (matching [arXiv 2203.04516: "less than half the update size of existing methods"](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.04516)), which at 300 kbps is **3–5 minutes per device** rather than 45+ minutes for a full image.

**Practical accuracy floor below 100 MB** is therefore not set by compression alone — it's set by **your mAP target on the custom dataset**. Compressing below 100 MB through pruning + INT8 + delta encoding does not intrinsically sacrifice measurable accuracy for these detector families; on a 50K-image warehouse set the realistic target band is:

| Model class | Realistic INT8-pruned mAP50-95 |
|---|---|
| YOLOv8n | 84–88% (40+ pp on small classes) |
| **YOLOv8s/m** | **88–92%** (the realistic ceiling without QAT) |
| DetectNet_v2 ResNet-34 (with QAT) | 89–93% (best ceiling for INT8) |
| EfficientDet-D0 | 80–85% |
| EfficientDet-D4 | 87–90% (better for small objects via BiFPN, but heavier to deploy) |

Reaching **>92% sustained mAP** on a warehouse set requires either:
- TAO DetectNet_v2 with QAT + domain-matched calibration, *or*
- YOLOv8 trained with simulated INT8 (NNCF, Brevitas, or open-source QAT tooling) — which is not in the Ultralytics mainline

This is a fact of **measurement, not of compression**. With pure PTQ on a COCO-calibrated engine applied to custom SKUs, 92% is borderline achievable; with QAT, it is routinely achievable.

---

## 6. TensorRT Optimization Gains: Where Are They Coming From?

The **2–3× TensorRT over PyTorch speedup** ([edgeaistack.ai YOLO TensorRT analysis](https://edgeaistack.ai/blog/yolo-tensorrt-jetson-fp16-vs-int8-2026/)) comes from three mechanisms:
1. **Layer fusion** — collapse Conv+BN+activation into single kernels
2. **Precision calibration** — INT8 on tensor cores gives 2–4× over FP16 once the engine is built
3. **Kernel auto-tuning** — picks the implementation specific to AGX Orin's 16 SMs (64GB SKU) or 7 TPCs (32GB SKU)

For multi-camera pipelines the practical gain compounds: TensorRT engines with DeepStream's batching sustain **2.5–3.5× the effective frame rate** of CPU-side ONNX Runtime or PyTorch on the same module, both because of layer fusion and because DeepStream manages decode + NMS + tracking on the dedicated hardware engines (NVENC for output, VIC for scaling, NVDEC for H.264/H.265 input). Without DeepStream you leave the camera decode pipeline CPU-bound.

**Operationally important traps:**
- **TensorRT 10.3 on JetPack 6 blocks INT8 end-to-end (NMS-included) engine builds** — upgrade to TensorRT 10.7+ via CUDA apt repo before going to INT8 ([edgeaistack.ai/.../blog/yolo-tensorrt-jetson-fp16-vs-int8-2026/](https://edgeaistack.ai/blog/yolo-tensorrt-jetson-fp16-vs-int8-2026/))
- **Engines are not portable** across modules — every AGX Orin 32GB vs 64GB vs Orin NX variant must rebuild its engine on the target hardware; building on a dev box and copying to fleet is the wrong pattern
- **Aggressive quantization only makes sense if you have the calibration data** — COCO calibration on warehouse data routinely costs 3–7 pp more mAP than domain-matched calibration

---

## 7. Edge Active Learning Loop: Can You Hit >92% Without Full Retraining?

**Yes — but only if you structure the loop carefully.** From the operational literature on closed-loop edge retraining ([Inferensys air-gapped loop](https://inferensys.com/train/edge-vision-model-quantization-and-distillation-for-industrial-deployment/active-learning-for-edge-model-retraining-pipelines/), [Maastricht Adaptive Retraining](https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/275137160/Winands-2025-Adaptive-Retraining-Techniques-for-Foreign.pdf), [MDPI rarity-aware AL](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/16/3/1236)):

**The architecture that works:**
1. **On-device uncertainty scoring** — on each module, compute least-confidence or margin-sampling metrics on every inference output (cheap: ~0.1 ms cost using the existing detection logits). Frames below a configurable threshold (top-1 confidence < 0.7, or margin between top-1 and top-2 < 0.15) are queued locally.
2. **Bandwidth-aware uplink** — pull batches of uncertain frames (and their detection metadata) to the central training server over cellular when the truck dock is open or during scheduled low-traffic windows. Typically 1–5% of the stream, not 100%.
3. **Class-stratified and rarity-aware sampling** — without explicit stratification, AL collapses on the long-tail of new SKUs ([MDPI 2026](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/16/3/1236) shows stratified AL retains >97% of mAP@50 of full supervision at 45–65% label budget).
4. **Targeted fine-tune, not full retrain** — for monthly SKU additions, **freeze the backbone, unfreeze only the head**, and run a small fine-tune (10–30 epochs) on the mixed old+new dataset. Empirical result for YOLOv8: deeper fine-tuning (down to layer 10) yields +10 pp on the new SKU with **<0.1 pp COCO degradation** ([arXiv 2505.01016](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.01016)).
5. **Canary + OTA + delta** — push the new model to 5–10% of the fleet first, validate accuracy over 48 hours, then roll out fleet-wide via the delta update mechanism (Oxide/Mallorn/TinyMLDelta pattern above).

**Where the >92% target does and doesn't hold:**

- **It is achievable for the existing-class retraining case** on a 50K-image dataset with backbone frozen, head unfrozen, and a class-replay buffer (~10% of old data kept in each fine-tune round). Empirically a YOLOv8m fine-tune retains ~98–99% of COCO performance and adds the new SKU to >92% on its own validation split.
- **It is *not* achievable for from-scratch class additions** without combining old + new training data (catastrophic forgetting kicks in aggressively when you only show the new SKU).
- **DetectNet_v2 with TAO's native workflow has an edge** — the same backbone-freeze, head-only fine-tune is a 3-line spec file change plus `load_graph=true`, whereas YOLOv8 requires Python-side surgery for the same outcome. The Neural Net Repository data and [TAO 4.0 add-new-classes whitepaper](https://developer.nvidia.com/tao-toolkit-usecases-whitepaper/4-add-new-classes-objects-existing-ai-model) document exactly this path.
- **Synthetic Active Learning (SAL)** is the closest published loop that doesn't need human-in-the-loop labeling at all — generates domain-randomized synthetic samples around detected failure modes. Reported +2 to +6 pp mAP@50 over static learning on manufacturing data ([Synthetic AL paper](https://exa.ai/library/publication/nvj6ck2tn7z)). Worth piloting if your SKU volume exceeds human review capacity.
- **Air-gapped compliance** is possible: an on-prem Jetson/Orin runs the uncertainty scorer, queues for review, and a local GPU cluster retrains. No cloud exfiltration needed ([Inferensys air-gapped flow](https://inferensys.com/train/edge-vision-model-quantization-and-distillation-for-industrial-deployment/active-learning-for-edge-model-retraining-pipelines/building-air-gapped-active-learning-pipelines-for-secure-industrial-vision-retraining)).

---

## 8. Side-by-Side Scorecard (Weighted for the Deployment Requirements)

| Criterion (weight) | YOLOv8s | EfficientDet-D4 | **DetectNet_v2 ResNet-34 pruned** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Throughput / module @ INT8 (25%)** | 9.1 cams | ~1.2 cams | **23.7 cams** |
| **mAP gap FP16→INT8, domain-matched (15%)** | 2–3 pp (PTQ) | 2–4 pp (PTQ) | **<1 pp (QAT optional)** |
| **Power per module sustained (10%)** | 22–32 W | Same envelope | 22–32 W (but 9 modules total) |
| **Per-frame inference energy (5%)** | 0.18 J (similar) | ~1.0 J | **0.04–0.10 J (lowest fleet total)** |
| **Model size under 100 MB after compression (10%)** | ~50 MB ✓ | ~75 MB ✓ (borderline) | **~30–45 MB ✓ (most headroom)** |
| **Incremental SKU update robustness (20%)** | Manual / fragile (catastrophic forgetting issues) | None | **TAO Pruning→Retrain→QAT→Export pipeline** |
| **OTA delta update friendliness (5%)** | ONNX/PyTorch → diffable via Oxide/Mallorn | TF saved_model (incompatible with most delta tooling) | **ETLT/ONNX → TAO-native diff-friendly** |
| **Active-learning ecosystem (10%)** | Generic Ultralytics training loop | None | **TAO AutoML + Active Learning integrations** |

**Winner for this deployment: TAO DetectNet_v2 (ResNet-34 backbone, pruned v2.3 variant).**

---

## 9. Concrete Recommendation

1. **Build on TAO DetectNet_v2 with ResNet-34 + pruning + QAT.** Train the base detection model on the 50K-image warehouse dataset in x86 with the TAO Toolkit. Apply channel pruning to roughly 50% sparsity, then retrain to recover accuracy, then enable QAT and retrain again. This compresses the production model to ~45 MB and keeps accuracy within 1 pp of FP16.
2. **Plan for ~9 Jetson AGX Orin 64GB modules** to cover 200 cameras at 30 fps, running one shared DetectNet_v2 model per module through DeepStream with batched inference. Confirm per-module throughput on your actual hardware before committing to the count — see the ±20% margin in the calculations above.
3. **Use DLA only for the lower-priority detection worker** (e.g., damage assessment at 5–10 Hz) so that the GPU can dedicate itself to label-reading at 30 fps.
4. **Active-learning loop:** on-device margin-sampling on every frame, queue locally, push only the bottom 1–5% of frames to an air-gapped or central training cluster. Monthly SKU additions: backbone frozen, head unfrozen, fine-tune for 10–30 epochs over the union of (10% old SKU buffer + new SKU). Aim for **mAP50-95 ≥ 92% on validation split, with classwise mAP ≥ 90% as the floor**.
5. **OTA:** use tensor-level delta updates (Oxide/Mallorn pattern) on top of the TensorRT engines. Patches will typically be 1–20 MB for an incremental SKU-add, comfortably cellular-friendly at LTE-M bitrates.
6. **TensorRT hygiene:** use TensorRT 10.7+ on JetPack 6, batch-engine-construction under `MAXN` power mode, rebuild engines on the actual deployment hardware. Budget 2.5–3.5 W per module reserved for sustained inference at 30 fps per stream and derate your PV / battery sizing accordingly if this is a renewable-powered site.

---

## 10. Honest Uncertainty Disclosure

- The Ultralytics-published INT8 FPS figures (342/248/107 for YOLOv8s/m/x on AGX Orin 64GB, MAXN, batch 1) are vendor-issued and at the optimistic end. Real deployments reach 70–85% of these numbers with decode/NMS overhead; plan module counts at the upper end of the range.
- EfficientDet-D4 measured FPS on AGX Orin 64GB at 640×640 was not independently published in the searches I performed; the 30–55 fps estimate is extrapolated from D0 (512×512) and T4 numbers. **Recommend a 24-hour on-device pilot to lock this number down before ruling EfficientDet in or out.**
- TAO DetectNet_v2 specific mAP degradation numbers on warehouse-specific datasets are not publicly tabulated; the "<1 pp" cited here is for QAT-retrained PeopleNet-class models on near-domain data. Pilot a representative fine-tune before committing the budget.
- The 92% mAP50-95 retention target via active learning comes from MDPI 2026 (rarity-aware stratified) and arXiv 2505.01016 (YOLOv8 layer-10 unfreeze) on datasets that are not warehouse-specific; treat 92% as the expected ceiling, not a guaranteed floor.

---

            tax += (top - prev) * rate

# As RRSP grows by rate r over n years
def rrsp_net_benefit(contribution, current_marg, future_marg, years, growth_rate, gross_up=1.0):
    """Compare after-tax value of $contribution going to RRSP vs TFSA"""
    # RRSP: contribute $X at marginal rate C, then grow at G, withdraw at rate F
    refund_at_contrib = contribution * current_marg
    equivalent_tfsa_contrib = contribution + refund_at_contrib  # tax-refund reinvested in TFSA
    # RRSP path: $contribution grows to X*(1+G)^n, taxed at F on withdrawal
    rrsp_value = contribution * ((1 + growth_rate) ** years)
    rrsp_after_tax = rrsp_value * (1 - future_marg) * gross_up
    # TFSA path: equivalent after-tax contribution grows tax-free
    tfsa_value = equivalent_tfsa_contrib * ((1 + growth_rate) ** years)
    return rrsp_after_tax, tfsa_value

        t, p = 0, 0
        for top, r in brackets:

                break
            else:

        return t
