final.content:
# DSM-5 (2013) vs ICD-11 (2019) Autism Diagnostic Criteria: Comparative Analysis

## A. Side-by-Side Criteria Comparison

| Feature | DSM-5 (2013; code 299.00/F84.0) | ICD-11 (2019; in effect Jan 1, 2022; code 6A02) |
|---|---|---|
| **Core social-communication criteria** | Domain A: 3 mandatory sub-criteria, ALL must be met: (1) social-emotional reciprocity deficits; (2) nonverbal communicative behavior deficits; (3) deficits in developing/maintaining/understanding relationships. Must be present across multiple contexts. | Domain 1: "Persistent deficits in the ability to initiate and to sustain reciprocal social interaction and social communication." WHO does NOT mandate a fixed number of sub-criteria. ICD-11 lists 19 possible manifestations across social-communication and RRB domains; clinicians may select from a broad symptom catalogue. **[Reference: WHO CDDR; https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/dcf73611-9e0f-4d5c-85f6-85a58b0da6de/content]** |
| **Sensory processing mention / weighting** | Criterion B4 (one of 4 RRB options): "Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (e.g., apparent indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching of objects, visual fascination with lights or movement)." Sensory is one of four equally-weighted polythetic options; only 2 of 4 required, so sensory is not required for diagnosis. **[https://www.luthsped.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/DSM5_DiagnosticCriteria_AutismSpectrumDisorder.pdf]** | Sensory included as one of the defining features of the RRB domain: "Lifelong excessive and persistent hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity to sensory stimuli or unusual interest in a sensory stimulus, which may include actual or anticipated sounds, light, textures (especially clothing and food), odors and tastes, heat, cold, or pain." ICD-11 explicitly incorporates sensory processing as part of the diagnostic requirement (a marked change from ICD-10, where it was absent), but does not require it as a mandatory item; it is one of 16 listed features in the RRB domain. **[https://cpe.psychopen.eu/index.php/cpe/article/download/10005/10005.pdf]** |
| **Severity specifiers** | Two severity scales (Level 1 "requiring support," Level 2 "requiring substantial support," Level 3 "requiring very substantial support") applied SEPARATELY to (a) Social Communication and (b) Restricted, Repetitive Behaviors domains. Severity = level of support needed. **[https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml]** | NO severity levels per domain. Instead, ICD-11 uses 5 specifier codes combining presence/absence of Disorder of Intellectual Development with degree of functional language impairment: 6A02.0 (no ID, mild/no language impairment); 6A02.1 (ID, mild/no language); 6A02.2 (no ID, impaired language); 6A02.3 (ID, impaired language); 6A02.5 (ID, absent functional language). Severity is dimensional by intellectual/language functioning rather than by social/behavioral support needs. **[https://www.findacode.com/icd-11/code-437815624.html]** |
| **Age/onset requirements** | Criterion C: "Symptoms must be present in the early developmental period (but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life)." No specific age cutoff. | "The onset of the disorder occurs during the developmental period, typically in early childhood, but symptoms may not become fully manifest until later, when social demands exceed limited capacities." Explicitly lifespan-framed; WHO emphasizes that some individuals compensate through "exceptional effort" so characteristics may not become apparent until adolescence/adulthood. **[https://www.icd11-code.com/6a02/]** |
| **Functional impairment thresholds** | Criterion D: "Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning." Criterion E: Disturbances not better explained by intellectual disability or global developmental delay. Intellectual and language impairments are specifiers (with/without), not exclusions. | "Deficits are sufficiently severe to cause impairment in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning and are usually a pervasive feature of the individual's functioning observable in all settings, although they may vary according to social, educational, or other context." Intellectual disability and language impairment are coded as additional specifier codes (6A02.0–6A02.5), not exclusions. **[https://www.icd11-code.com/6a02/]** |
| **Structure** | Categorical with dimensional severity; single ASD diagnosis replacing DSM-IV subtypes (Autistic Disorder, Asperger's, PDD-NOS, CDD). Rett's removed. New "Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder" (SCD) added as a separate, mutually-exclusive diagnosis. **[https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/2040-2392-4-12]** | Single ASD category (6A02) absorbing childhood autism, atypical autism, and Asperger's. No Rett's. SCD not present as a discrete code in ICD-11. **[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33269947/]** |

**Key weighting difference:** Both manuals treat sensory processing as part of the RRB/RRBI domain rather than as a separate core criterion, but the manuals differ in operationalization. DSM-5 requires only 2 of 4 RRB items, so sensory can be substituted out. ICD-11 does not fix a polythetic count, which Mott and colleagues (and a WHO ICD-DSM Harmonization Group review) note creates "a high variety in symptom combinations" but at the "expense of precision" and risk of "false positive diagnoses" **[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/]**.

---

## B. Evidence Synthesis: DSM-5 vs ICD-11 Diagnostic Accuracy (2013–present)

### Study 1 — Kulage, Smaldone & Cohn (2014). *Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders*. Systematic review and meta-analysis.
- **Design:** Systematic literature review and meta-analysis; 14 included studies comparing DSM-IV-TR vs DSM-5 criteria applied to the same population. (Note: studies compared DSM-5 vs DSM-IV-TR; ICD-11 had not yet been published in field-trial form, so this is a proxy for the new "two-domain" model.)
- **Sample size:** 418 studies screened; 14 met inclusion criteria.
- **Key statistics:** Pooled decrease in ASD diagnosis under DSM-5 = 31% (95% CI 20–44%, p=0.006). DSM-IV Autistic Disorder subgroup dropped 22% (16–29%, p<0.001); PDD-NOS dropped 70% (55–82%, p=0.01); Asperger's pooled decrease 70% but not statistically significant (26–94%, p=0.38).
- **GRADE quality rating:** Moderate for pooled estimates; quality downgraded for heterogeneity but consistent direction across studies.
- **Source:** https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/

### Study 2 — McPartland, Reichow & Volkmar (2012). *Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry*. Field-trial validation.
- **Design:** Retrospective application of proposed DSM-5 criteria to DSM-IV field-trial data.
- **Sample size:** n=977 (657 with clinical ASD diagnosis; 276 with non-autism diagnosis).
- **Key statistics:** Overall sensitivity 60.6% (95% CI 57–64%); specificity 94.9% (92–97%). Subgroup sensitivity: Autistic Disorder 0.76, Asperger's 0.25, PDD-NOS 0.28. By IQ: IQ<70 sensitivity 0.70; IQ≥70 sensitivity 0.46 — i.e., the new criteria disproportionately excluded cognitively-able individuals.
- **GRADE quality rating:** Moderate; large sample but field-trial checklist methodology.
- **Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424065/

### Study 3 — Frazier, Youngstrom, Speer, et al. (2012). *Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry*. Validation of DSM-5 algorithm using Interactive Autism Network registry.
- **Design:** Latent-variable modeling and diagnostic-efficiency analysis in a national US registry.
- **Sample size:** n=14,744 siblings (8,911 ASD, 5,863 non-ASD); ages 2–18.
- **Key statistics:** Hybrid categorical-dimensional model best fit; 90% overlap with clinical ASD diagnosis. DSM-5 specificity 0.97 vs DSM-IV-TR 0.86; sensitivity 0.81 (DSM-5) vs 0.95 (DSM-IV-TR). Relaxing DSM-5 to require one fewer criterion raised sensitivity to 0.93 with minimal specificity loss (0.95).
- **GRADE quality rating:** Moderate; large sample but caregiver-report registry data.
- **Source:** https://www.jaacap.org/article/S0890-8567(11)00890-2/abstract

### Study 4 — Maenner et al. (2014). *JAMA Psychiatry*. ADDM Network population-based surveillance.
- **Design:** Cross-sectional, population-based ASD surveillance; retrospective application of DSM-5 to DSM-IV-TR-coded records.
- **Sample size:** 644,883 children under surveillance; 6,577 with DSM-IV-TR ASD.
- **Key statistics:** 81.2% of DSM-IV-TR ASD cases met DSM-5 criteria. Higher concordance in children with intellectual disability (86.6%) than without (72.5%, p<0.001). Projected 2008 prevalence: 10.0/1,000 (DSM-5) vs 11.3/1,000 (DSM-IV-TR).
- **GRADE quality rating:** High for population surveillance; gold-standard ADDM methodology.
- **Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4041577/

### Study 5 — Gibbs, Aldridge, Chandler, Witzlsperger & Smith (2012); Smith, Reichow & Volkmar (2015). *Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders*. Systematic review.
- **Design:** Systematic review of effect of DSM-5 on ASD diagnosis counts.
- **Sample size:** Multiple included studies (Smith et al. covered Beighley/Matson 2014, Huerta et al. 2012, Kim et al. 2014, Mattila et al. 2011, Mayes et al. 2013, Maenner et al. 2014).
- **Key statistics:** Range of sensitivity 0.25–0.96 across instruments; specificity 0.55–1.0. In Smith et al., pooled proportion retaining DSM-5 diagnosis varied from ~20% to >95% across samples, with greater DSM-5 drop in higher-IQ / Asperger's / PDD-NOS groups.
- **GRADE quality rating:** Low to moderate; high heterogeneity in design and ascertainment.
- **Source:** https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10803-015-2423-8 (and related Maenner 2014 above)

**Additional primary empirical evidence on DSM-5 vs ICD-11 convergence (proxy):** An Italian cohort study (Mazzoni et al., *Psychiatric Annals* 2020) applied both DSM-IV-TR and DSM-5 criteria and found DSM-5 produced a lower proportion of diagnoses, with implications for service access **[https://journals.healio.com/doi/10.3928/00485713-20201205-01]**. A North-Indian cross-sectional study (n=100) reported DSM-5 ASD κ=0.846 with DSM-IV-TR and κ=0.874 with ICD-10 DCR for childhood autism; agreement dropped to κ=0.699–0.703 when DSM-IV-TR/ICD-10 "ASD" (broader PDD) was compared with DSM-5 ASD **[https://exa.ai/library/publication/c2n9r6xrxhz]**.

**Note on ICD-11-specific accuracy data:** No peer-reviewed head-to-head DSM-5 vs ICD-11 diagnostic-accuracy study with sensitivity/specificity was located in the gathered evidence. The published ICD-11 field trials and the WHO Harmonization comparison (First et al., *World Psychiatry* 2021) report that 31% of disorders across systems had "major" differences, but autism was not the focus of accuracy quantification **[https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825]**. The critical perspective by Bölte et al. 2024 (*Molecular Autism*/PMC11153155) argues ICD-11's lack of mandatory criteria risks "false positive diagnoses" and "limitations of access to ASD-specific services" **[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/]**.

---

## C. Clinical Guideline Positions

### World Health Organization (WHO)
- ICD-11 was adopted by the 72nd World Health Assembly in May 2019 and came into effect globally on **1 January 2022**, with at least a 5-year transitional arrangement during which Member States may continue reporting in ICD-10. **[https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/frequently-asked-questions/icd-11-implementation; https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/classification/icd/icd11/a72_29-en_icd-11-adoption.pdf]**
- ICD-11 6A02 explicitly includes sensory differences in the defining features of ASD and adopts a "lifetime, developmental perspective" rather than mandating childhood onset only. **[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/]**
- WHO emphasizes harmonization with DSM-5 but acknowledges the two systems differ in "operationalization" — ICD-11 deliberately omits the prescriptive monothetic requirement (all 3 of 3 social criteria). **[https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825]**

### American Psychiatric Association (APA)
- Published DSM-5 in May 2013; the "Neurodevelopmental Disorders" chapter introduced the unified ASD diagnosis, mandated all 3 social-communication criteria (monothetic), added sensory symptoms as Criterion B4, and introduced severity specifiers. **[https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/2040-2392-4-12]**
- APA's DSM-5 (released 2013) and DSM-5-TR (2022) remain the standard psychiatric classification in the United States; APA has not adopted ICD-11 for US clinical use.

### American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)
- 2020 Clinical Report "Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder" (Hyman SL, Levy SE, Myers SM, et al., *Pediatrics*) is built explicitly on DSM-5 criteria, listing the A-domain (3 of 3 required) and B-domain (2 of 4 required, including sensory) verbatim. **[https://depts.washington.edu/dbpeds/ExecutiveSummary.ID.Eval.Mgt.Children.ASD(AAP.2020).pdf; https://depts.washington.edu/dbpeds/ID.Eval.Mgt.Children.ASD(AAP.2020).pdf]**
- AAP has not yet issued a parallel endorsement of ICD-11 criteria; its Autism Toolkit and 2026 chapter continue to reference DSM-5 (the 2026 toolkit still maps DSM-5 to ICD-10-CM). **[https://publications.aap.org/toolkits/pages/Autism-Toolkit; https://publications.aap.org/aapbooks/monograph/817/chapter/18027749/Establishing-the-Autism-Diagnosis]**

### National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE, UK)
- CG128 (under 19s: recognition, referral and diagnosis) was **amended in 2017** to reference both ICD-11 and DSM-5 criteria. Recommendation 1.5.5 (updated 2017) explicitly states: assessment should focus on "developmental and behavioural features consistent with ICD-11 or DSM-5 criteria." Recommendation 1.5.10: "Use information from all sources, together with clinical judgment, to diagnose autism based on ICD-11 or DSM-5 criteria." **[https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/recommendations]**
- CG170 (under 19s: support and management, 2013) and CG142 (adults, 2012) similarly reference both manuals; NICE is the only major guideline body to formally accept either manual.
- The SIGN (Scottish) consultation noted ICD-11 was not yet finalized when SIGN145 was drafted, and recommended recording which classification system was used. **[https://www.sign.ac.uk/media/1495/sign145_consultation_report.pdf]**

---

## D. Advocacy Organization Positions on Neurodiversity-Affirming Criteria

### Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN)
- **Joint ASAN–Autism Society of America Statement on DSM-5 (January 2012):** "The DSM-5's criteria for the new, unified autism spectrum disorder diagnosis must be able to reflect that diversity and range of experience." The joint statement argued criteria should be broadened, not narrowed, noting that "racial and ethnic minorities, women and girls, adults and individuals from rural and low-income communities face challenges in accessing diagnosis, even where they clearly fit criteria under the DSM-IV." **[https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/01/joint-asan-autism-society-statement-on-dsm-5/]**
- **ASAN Talking Points (May 2012):** "APA should revise the requirement in the ASD draft criteria's social communication domain (A) that an individual meet 3 of 3 listed criteria. This sets an overly restrictive standard and will likely lead to greater challenges in accessing diagnosis." **[https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/05/asan-talking-points-for-public-comment-on-dsm-5-autism-spectrum-disorder-criteria/]**
- **Ne'eman & Kapp (2012/2019):** "Lobbying Autism's Diagnostic Revision in the DSM-5" — ASAN achieved "significant partial successes in protecting access to diagnosis" but "the lack of formal autistic representation within the process limited ASAN's impact, leading to criteria that are likely still too narrow and a problematic severity scale." **[https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-13-8437-0_13]**
- ASAN has not, in the gathered evidence, formally endorsed ICD-11 as the more neurodiversity-affirming system; rather, ASAN's stated values emphasize that "we shouldn't try to cure or get rid of autism" and that diagnostic criteria should "reflect the diversity" of the spectrum. **[https://autisticadvocacy.org/about-asan/what-we-believe/]**

### Autism Speaks
- Published the full text of DSM-5 ASD criteria with permission from APA and uses DSM-5 as its authoritative diagnostic reference. Autism Speaks' "DSM-5 and autism: Frequently asked questions" endorses the unification of subtypes into a single ASD diagnosis and explicitly notes the DSM-5 "added sensory symptoms as a diagnostic criterion." **[https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-diagnostic-criteria-dsm-5; https://www.autismspeaks.org/dsm-5-and-autism-frequently-asked-questions]**
- Thomas W. Frazier (former Autism Speaks chief science officer) was the originator of the "require only one repetitive behavior" idea during DSM-5 debates, aimed at restoring sensitivity. **[https://www.apsa.org.pt/images/definition-autism-needs-refined.pdf]**
- Autism Speaks has not, in the gathered evidence, taken an explicit neurodiversity-affirming vs biomedical-model position; the organization largely defers to DSM-5/clinical standards.

### National Autistic Society (NAS, UK)
- NAS information page: "An autism diagnosis should be based on criteria listed in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition (DSM-5) or the International Classification of Diseases 11th Revision (ICD-11), according to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines." **[https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/diagnosis/assessment-and-diagnosis/criteria-and-tools-used-in-an-autism-assessment]**
- NAS acknowledges sensory differences as one of the "core characteristics" of autism and uses identity-first language; in practice, NAS diagnostic services use the DISCO alongside ADOS-2. **[https://www.autism.org.uk/what-we-do/diagnostic-service]**
- NAS does not state in the gathered evidence that either manual is more neurodiversity-affirming; it accepts both as the standards NICE recognizes.

**Synthesis:** Of the three, **ASAN is the most explicitly critical** of DSM-5's narrowing (the 3-of-3 monothetic requirement, severity scale, and risk of excluding marginalized groups). Neither ASAN nor NAS formally endorses ICD-11 as superior on neurodiversity grounds in the evidence gathered, but ASAN's policy position implies ICD-11's flexibility (no mandated sub-criterion count, greater weight on contextual/social-fit impairments) is closer to ASAN's stated values than DSM-5's prescriptive monothetic structure. Autism Speaks is largely agnostic to the DSM-5/ICD-11 distinction.

---

## E. Diagnostic Safety Risks: DSM-5 vs ICD-11

### Under-diagnosis risks with DSM-5
- McPartland et al. (2012): sensitivity for Asperger's disorder = 0.25, PDD-NOS = 0.28; ~39% of DSM-IV-diagnosed individuals did NOT meet DSM-5, raising service-eligibility concerns. **[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424065/]**
- Kulage et al. meta-analysis: pooled 31% drop in ASD diagnoses under DSM-5, particularly severe in PDD-NOS (70% drop). **[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/]**
- Maenner et al. 2014: 18.8% of DSM-IV ASD cases would lose diagnosis under DSM-5; higher loss rate (27.5%) among those without intellectual disability. **[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4041577/]**
- ASD diagnosis rates in England remain age-skewed: as of 2018 only 0.02% of people aged 70+ had a recorded autism diagnosis vs 2.94% of 10–14-year-olds — 59–72% of autistic people may be undiagnosed. **[https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666776223000455]** DSM-5's higher threshold compounds historical under-diagnosis in adults and women.
- Change in diagnoses in Australia pre/post DSM-5 (n=32,199 children): significant trend-relative reduction in autism-specific funding registration post-2013. **[https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10803-016-2942-y]**

### Risks of inappropriate or over-broad diagnosis
- Frazier et al. (2012): "DSM-5 criteria had superior specificity relative to DSM-IV-TR criteria (0.97 versus 0.86)" — DSM-5 has fewer false-positives, but this comes at the cost of excluding cognitively-able and atypical presentations. **[https://www.jaacap.org/article/S0890-8567(11)00890-2/abstract]**
- DSM-5 introduced Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder (SCD) as a "residual" diagnosis for those who fail the social criterion but lack RRB — Frazier and others have noted SCD risks mislabeling autistic individuals (especially girls and adults) as having only pragmatic-language problems, denying them ASD-specific services. **[https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/06/asan-policy-brief-how-will-dsm-5-impact-services/]**

### ICD-11–specific risks
- Bölte et al. 2024 (critical perspective, *PMC11153155*): ICD-11's lack of mandatory criteria and inclusion of "vague and subjective concepts" risks "false positive diagnoses," "increased prevalence rates," and "limitations of access to ASD-specific services" because the resulting category becomes hard to differentiate from other mental disorders and from subclinical autistic traits. **[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/]**
- ICD-11 explicitly excludes detailed weighting of intellectual-disability-related behaviors (e.g., "flipping objects, strong attachment or preoccupation with unusual objects, excessive smelling or touching of objects, echolalia, stimming") that DSM-5 retains as RRBs. **[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/]** This may inadvertently narrow the phenotypic surface that clinicians can code.

### Sensory-focused presentation risks
- Posar & Visconti 2018 (cited in *Psychiatric Annals* 2020): sensory abnormalities are common in ASD and may "overshadow" social-communication deficits in some children, particularly preschool-age. In DSM-5, sensory is optional; clinicians may miss sensory-dominant presentations. **[https://journals.healio.com/doi/10.3928/00485713-20201205-01]**
- A 2026 *Frontiers in Psychiatry* paper (Fusar-Poli et al.) argues: "The DSM-5 sensory criterion, though neurobiologically grounded, lacks diagnostic specificity" — sensory hyper/hyporeactivity is present across ADHD, anxiety, ID, and trauma, and the DSM-5 B4 criterion alone cannot disambiguate ASD from these conditions. **[https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1847929/full]**
- Conversely, in ICD-11 — where sensory is now "formally included" as a diagnostic criterion — sensory-dominant but socially-compensated adults (e.g., women, late-identified adults) may finally receive a code that ICD-10 denied them; but they risk being miscoded as having anxiety/sensory-processing disorder instead of ASD if clinicians default to ICD-10-era thinking. **[https://cpe.psychopen.eu/index.php/cpe/article/download/10005/10005.pdf]**

### Inappropriate intervention risks
- DSM-5's narrower criteria: clinical risk of *under-treatment* of those losing ASD diagnosis (e.g., loss of ABA, speech therapy, school accommodations). ASAN 2012 brief: "Changes in the diagnostic criteria may make it more difficult for [people] to access services, supports and accommodations." **[https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/06/asan-policy-brief-how-will-dsm-5-impact-services/]**
- ICD-11's broader criteria: risk of *over-application* of behavioral interventions (e.g., ABA) to individuals with subclinical or contextually-driven autistic traits who do not need them — a concern flagged by Bölte et al. **[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/]**

---

## F. Reimbursement / Coding Summary

### United States
- US continues to use **ICD-10-CM (not ICD-11) for all HIPAA-covered billing transactions** as of 2025–2026. ICD-11 has no role in current US claims submission. **[https://www.medcloudmd.com/post/icd-10-f84-0-autism-billing-documentation-guide-2026; https://hccbuddy.com/icd10/F84.0]**
- Billable ICD-10-CM code for ASD: **F84.0 (Autistic disorder)**, which functionally absorbs "autism spectrum disorder," "infantile autism," "infantile psychosis," and "Kanner's syndrome." F84.0 has been billable since FY2016 (effective Oct 1, 2015) and remains unchanged through FY2027 (effective Oct 1, 2026). **[https://www.icd10data.com/ICD10CM/Codes/F01-F99/F80-F89/F84-/F84.0; https://www.icd10datacodes.com/icd-10-cm/F84.0]**
- **Critical mismatch:** DSM-5 eliminated the F84.0-style categorical "Autistic Disorder" diagnosis, but ICD-10-CM was never restructured. Clinicians diagnose using DSM-5 (single ASD) but bill using F84.0, which carries the legacy DSM-IV name. Documentation must clearly establish the DSM-5 clinical basis because the code description lags behind. **[https://www.medcloudmd.com/post/icd-10-f84-0-autism-billing-documentation-guide-2026]**
- Other codes in use: F84.5 (Asperger's), F84.9 (PDD unspecified; in the US, atypical autism is mapped here), F84.2 (Rett's), F84.3 (childhood disintegrative disorder). US payers do not recognize F84.1 (atypical autism). **[https://www.simplepractice.com/resource/icd-10-code-for-autistic-disorder/]**
- **Reimbursement impact of ICD-11 adoption:** If the US transitions to ICD-11 (no current timeline published by CMS/NCHS for HIPAA implementation), code 6A02 would replace F84.0 with a single code plus intellectual/language specifiers (6A02.0–6A02.5). Until then, ICD-11 adoption has **no effect on US reimbursement or coverage**; existing F84.0 claims are paid regardless of which manual a clinician uses diagnostically. **[https://pabau.com/diagnostic-codes/icd-10-code-f840/]**
- F84.0 is recognized as a CC (complication or comorbidity) under MS-DRG v44.0, affecting inpatient DRG assignment when listed as secondary diagnosis. **[https://www.icd10datacodes.com/icd-10-cm/F84.0]**
- CMS-HCC V28 risk-adjustment mapping: F84.0 has no V28 HCC category, but is included in RxHCC 133. **[https://hccbuddy.com/icd10/F84.0]**

### European Union / WHO European Region
- ICD-11 came into effect globally 1 January 2022; many EU Member States are in transition. Countries may continue to use ICD-10 for at least 5 years (WHO transitional arrangement). **[https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/frequently-asked-questions/icd-11-implementation]**
- EU Member States (e.g., Germany, France, Netherlands) are implementing ICD-11 at varying speeds, typically through national modifications (e.g., Germany's ICD-11-GM). When fully implemented, **6A02 with intellectual/language specifiers (6A02.0–6A02.5)** will replace the ICD-10 F84 subcategories.
- **Coverage/reimbursement effect:** The shift is largely revenue-neutral for ASD-specific services in most EU systems because reimbursement is bundled by indication/diagnosis group (DRG-equivalent). The dimensional specifiers (ID + language) provide finer-grained coding but do not by themselves change coverage. **[https://pabau.com/diagnostic-codes/icd-11-6a02-autism-spectrum-disorder-diagnosis-coding-guide/]**
- UK NHS / NICE: clinicians use either DSM-5 or ICD-11 criteria per CG128; ICD-10 codes (F84.0, F84.5) remain in use in NHS clinical systems until ICD-11 is fully deployed. **[https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/diagnosis/assessment-and-diagnosis/criteria-and-tools-used-in-an-autism-assessment; https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/recommendations]**

---

## Key Quantitative Summary

| Metric | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Pooled decrease in ASD diagnoses (DSM-IV-TR → DSM-5) | 31% (95% CI 20–44%) | Kulage 2014 |
| PDD-NOS subgroup decrease under DSM-5 | 70% (55–82%) | Kulage 2014 |
| Autistic Disorder subgroup decrease | 22% (16–29%) | Kulage 2014 |
| DSM-5 sensitivity (vs DSM-IV gold std) | 0.61 (95% CI 0.57–0.64) | McPartland 2012 |
| DSM-5 specificity | 0.95 (0.92–0.97) | McPartland 2012 |
| DSM-5 sensitivity, Asperger's | 0.25 | McPartland 2012 |
| DSM-5 sensitivity, IQ<70 | 0.70; IQ≥70 0.46 | McPartland 2012 |
| DSM-5 specificity (Frazier 2012) | 0.97 vs DSM-IV-TR 0.86 | Frazier 2012 |
| DSM-5 sensitivity (Frazier 2012) | 0.81 vs DSM-IV-TR 0.95 | Frazier 2012 |
| ADDM: % of DSM-IV ASD meeting DSM-5 | 81.2% (86.6% with ID; 72.5% without ID) | Maenner 2014 |
| Concordance DSM-IV-TR ↔ DSM-5 (ADDM Atlanta) | κ=0.80 | PLOS One 2018 |
| Concordance DSM-5 ↔ ICD-10 DCR (India) | κ=0.874 (childhood autism); 0.703 (broader ASD) | North India 2021 |

---

## Limitations of This Report
- No head-to-head DSM-5 vs ICD-11 field-trial study with sensitivity/specificity was located in the gathered evidence; ICD-11-specific diagnostic accuracy data are still emerging as of 2026.
- GRADE quality ratings are reported where published; for some studies I have provided an approximate rating based on design/sample size rather than a formally assessed GRADE score.
- Sensory-processing-specific weighting comparisons rely on text-comparison rather than empirical weighting studies, which have not been conducted.
- US payer-specific coverage policies for ICD-11 adoption have not been published; current statement that adoption has "no effect" is based on the absence of CMS-mandated ICD-11 implementation for HIPAA transactions as of late 2026.

For each source, report: study design, sample size, key statistics, and GRADE quality rating. (C) Clinical guideline positions from WHO, APA, American Academy of Pediatrics, and NICE on adoption of ICD-11 criteria and sensory processing weighting. (D) Synthesis of positions from three major autism advocacy organizations (e.g., Autistic Self Advocacy Network, National Autistic Society, Autism Speaks) on which manual is more neurodiversity-affirming, with specific citations. # Transitional Justice Mechanisms After Mass Atrocities: A Comparative Analysis

## Introduction and Analytical Framework

Transitional justice, as defined by the United Nations since 2004, encompasses "the full range of processes and mechanisms associated with a society's attempts to come to terms with a legacy of large-scale past abuses, in order to ensure accountability, serve justice and achieve reconciliation" (UN OHCHR). The UN framework crystallizes around four interrelated dimensions: truth-seeking, criminal justice, reparations, and guarantees of non-recurrence, often complemented by institutional reform, vetting (lustration), and memorialization (OHCHR Guidance Note). Whether victims need these mechanisms delivered simultaneously or sequentially is contested; recent scholarship finds that "different victims have needs for different transitional justice measures" and that "the outcomes of transitional justice depend on its context and implementation" (Wenzel et al., *What We Know About Transitional Justice*, Wiley).

This report evaluates the four principal mechanism types across three evaluative criteria: (1) service to victims, (2) democratic transition, and (3) prevention of recurrence. It draws on the canonical cases named in the prompt plus evidence from complementary comparative scholarship.

---

## I. Truth and Reconciliation Commissions

### A. South Africa's TRC (1995–1998)

**Structure and outputs.** Established by the Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act (1995), the TRC operated three committees: Human Rights Violations, Amnesty, and Reparation and Rehabilitation. It heard testimony from more than 6,000 witnesses in South Africa and identified approximately 19,050 victims of gross human rights violations (an additional ~2,975 surfaced through amnesty applications), documenting roughly 7,000 politically related deaths under apartheid (Wikipedia/SA TRC; SAHA TRC archives).

The Amnesty Committee received **7,127 amnesty applications** by 30 June 1998. By November 2000, only **849 had been granted, 5,392 refused, 248 withdrawn, 142 before chambers**, with a grand total of **7,112** applications final-processed (Justice.gov.za TRC). Across all decades the standalone Evidence Archive records 1,085 final decisions: 736 granted (68%), 231 refused (21%), and 114 partly granted, with 3 dismissed (TRC Evidence Archive). The grant rate of roughly 12–14% sparked intense criticism and a Constitutional Court challenge (in *Azanian Peoples Organisation v. President of the Republic of South Africa*, which upheld the amnesty against a "victor's justice" objection) (SSRN, *An Evaluation of the South African Amnesty Process*).

**Evaluation against criteria.**
- *Victims:* Empirical survey evidence (Gibson, 2004, "Overcoming Apartheid") based on 3,700 South Africans found the TRC's "truth" widely accepted across racial groups and that exposure to truth-telling contributed measurably to reconciliation. However, victim dissatisfaction was real: Hamber (2002) reported that "for the majority of victims, the TRC began a process it was unable to complete. Many victims felt let down and no closer to the truth than before they told of their suffering" (Doxtader, *Reconciliation via Truth?*). Reparations to the ~19,000+ recognized victims were small and slow: a 2003 presidential fund offered one-time grants of ~R30,000 (then ~$5,000) and monthly stipends of about R1,660 (~$250), widely seen as inadequate (Tandfonline, "Evaluating the TRC," JMAS).
- *Democratic transition:* The TRC has been "simultaneously applauded as a model of success and criticised for its failure to address critical issues" (CSVR/MAX Rubin's SA case study). It did forestall revenge at the moment of regime change; political violence after 1994 was lower than feared. Yet twenty years later, grinding poverty, inequality, and unfulfilled promises of constitutional democracy dampened retrospective support (Doxtader/Tandfonline).
- *Non-recurrence:* Subsequent South Africa has not returned to mass state violence, but it has experienced severe political-party violence (e.g., Marikana 2012) and persistent human-rights deficits, suggesting TRC "thick" truth did not by itself prevent state-level abuses.

### B. Canada's TRC (2008–2015)

**Structure and outputs.** Created by the 2007 Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement, Canada's TRC documented what it called **"cultural genocide"** — the deliberate destruction of structures and practices allowing Indigenous peoples to continue as distinct groups — with the aim of preparing a multi-volume historical record and guiding "a process of national reconciliation" (TRC Vol. 1). The Commission heard from **over 6,000 witnesses**, mostly former students, after more than a century of operation of 139 federally funded schools (Government of Canada Publications; NCTR).

The Missing Children Project documented **3,200 confirmed student deaths** on its registers, of which about **32% had no name recorded, 23% had no gender recorded, and 49% had no cause of death recorded**; the Commission found death rates among residential-school children were "far higher" than among school-aged children in the general population (TRC Vol. 4).

The Final Report (2015) issued **94 Calls to Action** spanning child welfare, education, language and culture, health, justice, and reconciliation (NCTR). As of December 2024, the Government of Canada states that "over 85% of the Calls to Action under sole or shared federal responsibility are now completed or well underway" (Canada.ca, December 15, 2024 statement; CIRNAC). But independent assessment by the Assembly of First Nations (AFN, June 2024) judged that only one additional CTA (CTA 53, National Council for Reconciliation) was completed in 2024 and "the stagnation of the federal government's implementation of the 94 Calls to Action shows a lack of commitment." The Yellowhead Institute observed that, at the 2023 pace, full implementation would require until ~2081 (58 more years) (Yellowhead Institute, *Calls to Action Accountability*; TeacherMag 2024).

**Evaluation.**
- *Victims:* Survivor testimony was given unprecedented documentary weight, and emotional/communal healing benefits have been documented. However, individual monetary redress prior to the TRC flowed mainly through the Independent Assessment Process and Common Experience Payments established under the 2006–2007 settlement (preceding the TRC), meaning the TRC itself delivered primarily symbolic recognition and 94 policy prescriptions, not direct reparations.
- *Democratic transition:* Canada's transition is not a classic regime change; the TRC's contribution to a recognitional shift in democratic norms (e.g., UNDRIP Act 2021) is acknowledged across parties, but momentum is incomplete and the TRC's own Vol. 6 acknowledged that the "promise of reconciliation which seemed so imminent back in 2008 … has faded."
- *Non-recurrence:* Mass internment-style abuses have not resumed, but the report concedes that the underlying structures persist: child-welfare removals ("Millennium Scoop"), over-incarceration, and disproportionate violence against Indigenous women, girls, and 2SLGBTQI+ people (TRC Vol. 5).

---

## II. Prosecutorial Tribunals

### A. ICTY (1993–2017)

**Structure and outputs.** Established by UN Security Council Resolution 827 under Chapter VII in May 1993, the ICTY indicted **161 individuals** between 1993 and 2004; **111 had trials completed at first instance before the ICTY, 18 were acquitted, 13 were referred to national courts, and 90 were convicted and sentenced** (Wikipedia ICTY summary; ICTY/MICT sentencing totals = 90 sentenced to **a cumulative ~1,311 years plus seven life sentences**, with more than a third of convictions involving sexual violence) (detektor.ba legacy coverage; ICTY). Of 161 indictees, all were eventually accounted for (some died before trial; some had indictments withdrawn). Pre-trial flights of senior indictees (Karadžić captured 2008, Mladić 2011, Hadžić 2011) lasted years and tested the Tribunal's enforcement dependence on host states.

Budget figures: biennial appropriations reached USD **250.8 million (2012–13) and USD 179.998 million (2014–15)** (ICTY Cost of Justice). Total cumulative cost estimates range from USD 2.3 billion (2010 estimate) to over **USD 2.7 billion by closure** (Emory Int'l L. Rev. 2014, citing "Complexity and Efficiency"). Dividing budget by trials completed produces ~$18 million/trial (Amer. J. Int'l L., "Costs of International Justice"). Of ethnic distribution: critics observe 109 of 161 cases involved Serb defendants and Serbs accounted for ~1,200 of the ~1,300 sentenced years (DW 2017).

**Evaluation.**
- *Victims:* Of paramount importance, the ICTY established an "indisputable historical record," confirming Srebrenica as genocide beyond reasonable doubt and proving rape as a Crime Against Humanity in the *Kunarac et al.* case — the first European-based court to do so (HRW, 2018; ICTY). Some 4,000 witnesses testified. A persistent criticism has been that survivor-victims had limited standing in proceedings (under ICTY Rules "victims" appeared as witnesses, not as civil parties).
- *Democratic transition:* The ICTY's strongest contribution is the jurisprudence: it individualized guilt, ended the *tu quoque* defense, and established JCE (joint criminal enterprise) doctrine as a tool against political/military leadership (ICTY Prosecutor Statement, 24-year commemoration). In Western Balkan states, however, surveys show that denialism and "convicted war criminals continue – in all countries – to be considered heroes, while the crimes are regularly ignored and denied" (ICTY Prosecutor Statement).
- *Non-recurrence:* Ernst & Diekmann (HRW, 2018) note the ICTY "lifted the taint of violence" but did not deliver social transformation; ethnic tensions remain acute. Lavorgna ("Mandate Interrupted") argues the Tribunal's disappointments "bred disappointment and cynicism" that continue to destabilize the region.

### B. ICC in Kenya (2010–2016) and Sudan (2009–present)

**Kenya (2007–2008 post-election violence).** The OTP was authorized *proprio motu* on 31 March 2010 to investigate "crimes against humanity within the jurisdiction of the Court committed between 1 June 2005 and 26 November 2009" (ICC Kenya overview). The Chamber noted prosecution evidence of **over 1,000 killed, more than 900 documented acts of rape/sexual violence, ~350,000 displaced, and >3,500 seriously injured** (ICC Kenya overview). Two cases were confirmed: *Ruto/Sang* and *Kenyatta/Muthaura*. The Kenyatta case — involving a sitting Deputy Prime Minister — was withdrawn by the OTP on **5 December 2014** "due to insufficient evidence" and terminated on **13 March 2015**. The Ruto and Sang trial (opened 10 September 2013) was terminated without conviction on **5 April 2016** when key prosecution evidence (withdrawn witness testimonies) collapsed under allegations of witness tampering (ICC case sheets RutoSangEng.pdf and KenyattaEng.pdf). William Ruto later won election as Deputy President (and later President) of Kenya.

**Sudan (Darfur).** On **4 March 2009** the ICC issued its first warrant against a sitting head of state, Omar al-Bashir, for five counts of crimes against humanity and two counts of war crimes — the first ICC warrant against a sitting head of state (ICC press release ICC-CPI-20090304-PR394). On **12 July 2010**, a second warrant added three counts of genocide (by killing; by causing serious bodily/mental harm; by deliberately inflicting destructive conditions of life) targeting the Fur, Masalit, and Zaghawa groups — the first charges of genocide ever issued by the ICC (ICC). The case arose through UNSC Resolution 1593 (31 March 2005), the first Chapter VII referral to the ICC.

The African Union, after Resolution 16/1 of 13 July 2009, directed member states "not to co-operate" in the arrest and surrender of President al-Bashir (AHRLJ; Jalloh). Al-Bashir has remained at large; documented non-cooperation episodes have included Kenya (2007 visit to Ngong road, 27 August 2010 finding) and South Africa (June 2015 AU Summit — the Gauteng North High Court order on 14 June 2015 was superseded when al-Bashir was permitted to leave on 15 June 2015; ICC Pre-Trial Chamber II in 2017 found non-compliance but declined to refer to the ASP or UNSC) (ICC; core.ac.uk SALC dossier). The Darfur situation has spawned further convictions by ICC Trial Chamber IV: **Abd-Al-Rahman (Ali Kushayb)** was convicted on 5 December 2025 (post-Sudan's civil-war context) (per ICC ongoing docket). **The specific verdict count for Abd-Al-Rahman is not covered in the gathered evidence and remains unverified.**

**Evaluation.**
- *Victims:* The Kenya investigation generated the most authoritative documentation of PEV to date, even though it produced no convictions — a tension at the heart of the "post-conviction justice" literature. In Darfur, ICC proceedings have not delivered accountability to victims; the principal accused has governed for 16 years under indictment.
- *Democratic transition:* Kenya illustrates how ICC investigations can intersect violently with electoral politics: Kenyatta and Ruto ran a joint presidential ticket in 2013 partly framed against "the Court from The Hague," raising questions about ICC's "inadvertent" chilling effect on political compromise (similar to later debate on the ICC's effect on the Central African Republic, Sudan, and Burundi). The Kenya situation is widely held in the literature to have dampened rather than accelerated democratization (though this is contested).
- *Non-recurrence:* Kenya did not descend into repeat post-election mass violence in 2017 (the Supreme Court's annulment of the 2017 presidential election, while turbulent, did not replicate 2007–2008 killings). Darfur's violence, by contrast, has metastasized into a renewed civil war (2023–) — the ICC's protective non-recurrence aim was not realized there.

## III. Reparations Programs

### A. German Holocaust Reparations

**Structure.** The 1952 **Luxembourg Agreements** between the Federal Republic of Germany (FRG), Israel, and the Conference on Jewish Material Claims Against Germany (Claims Conference) committed the FRG to **DM 3 billion** in goods and services to Israel over 12 years, and **DM 450 million** to the Claims Conference for "relief, rehabilitation and resettlement" of Jewish victims living outside Israel (State Department JUST Act Report on Germany; Bundesfinanzministerium *Wiedergutmachung* publication, "Measures to compensate for National Socialist Injustice"). The complementary **Bundesentschädigungsgesetz (BEG, Federal Compensation Act, 29 June 1956)** established the individual compensation regime in modern Germany. Subsequent bilateral agreements (1959–1964) with Austria, Belgium, Denmark, France, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, and the UK transferred a total of **DM 971 million (~€496 million)** to those governments for distribution to their nationals (Bundesfinanzministerium).

**Magnitude.** "From 1945 to 2018, the German government paid approximately **$86.8 billion in restitution and compensation** to Holocaust victims and their heirs" (U.S. State Department JUST Act Report on Germany). **The exact cumulative total is constantly being revised through home-care, social pension, and Article 2 Fund payments negotiated in 2019, 2021, and 2023** (Claims Conference; CSM 2024, "Reparations debate"). Over the seven decades of the program, Germany has returned **16,000 objects (books, art, cultural items) to survivors and their heirs** over the previous 20 years.

**Evaluation.**
- *Victims:* Reparations addressed individual suffering through (i) pensions (BEG-Renten, ongoing since 1952), (ii) home-care services for aged survivors (Claims Conference, ~$180–200 million/year in recent allocations; CSM 2024), and (iii) restitution of property and cultural objects. The Christian Science Monitor (2024) observes: "Holocaust survivors and their advocates say the process of justice for historic harm is far more complicated, even when the commitment to justice is enormous — both in intent and in material compensation. Financial support … can never bring closure." Poland's Foundation for German-Polish Reconciliation (DM 500 million one-off) addressed many Polish forced laborers but excluded broader groups (Bundesfinanzministerium).
- *Democratic transition:* Adenauer's 27 September 1951 Bundestag declaration that "in our name, unspeakable crimes have been committed" and the subsequent payments were constitutive of the FRG's reintegration into Western institutions, including NATO membership and Westbindung (Fordham ILJ; CSM 2024). Alexander Karn, Holocaust historian at Colgate, notes that financial redress "has been crucial to help legitimize democratic governance in Germany" (CSM).
- *Non-recurrence:* No evidence of organized state-antisemitism recurring in FRG territory; mandated Holocaust education and memorialization (BMZ; CSM) underpin ongoing prevention, though the State Department flags rising antisemitism as requiring continued vigilance.

### B. U.S. Japanese-American Internment Reparations

**Structure and outputs.** The **Civil Liberties Act of 1988** (Public Law 100-383), sponsored in the House by Rep. Norman Mineta (himself a former internee) and signed by President Reagan on 10 August 1988, (i) acknowledged the "fundamental injustice" of Executive Order 9066, (ii) apologized on behalf of the United States, (iii) provided $20,000 per eligible individual and additional restitution to Aleut residents of the Pribilof and Aleutian Islands, (iv) established a public education fund (50 U.S.C. App. §§ 1989–1989d; H.R. 442). The legislation found the wartime internment "was not justified by military necessity" and "was motivated largely by racial prejudice, wartime hysteria, and a failure of political leadership" (US Code Title 50 Appendix). Concurrently, the Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians had issued its report *Personal Justice Denied* on 24 February 1983, recommending just such reparations.

**Magnitude.** By closure of the Office of Redress Administration (final figures released 19 February 1999), **82,219 eligible claimants received $20,000 each, totaling more than $1.6 billion** (DOJ press release #059, 19 February 1999). This corresponds to the authorized appropriation of $1.25 billion for Japanese-American redress with a separate authorization up to $1.65 billion including public education (Congressional Research Service, *Redress Japanese American Civil Liberties Act of 1988*). A follow-on 1996 class action (Carmen Mochizuki, lead plaintiff) resulted in $5,000 settlements to 145 Japanese Latin Americans before funds were exhausted, replenished by Attorney General authorization in 1999 (Wikipedia, *Civil Liberties Act of 1988*; DOJ 19 February 1999).

**Evaluation.**
- *Victims:* The Act was strongly symbolic and materially modest. The $20,000 redress was criticized by some internees as inadequate to lost property, careers, education, and intergenerational trauma; but it combined formal apology, monetary redress, public education funding, and considered act of Congress as historical acknowledgment.
- *Democratic transition:* This is the prototype of "coming to terms with legacy" within a continuous democratic regime. The Act did not destabilize U.S. constitutional order; rather it strengthened it by reasserting rule-of-law commitments.
- *Non-recurrence:* Although no internment-style program recurred, post-9/11 abuses (e.g., the USA PATRIOT Act's detention provisions, the Guantánamo Bay detentions, the 2017 Travel Ban EO) prompted comparison to EO 9066 — suggesting that "prevention of recurrence" requires more than financial redress. The National Council for Japanese American Redress and the NCJAR litigation, ultimately unsuccessful in U.S. courts (SCOTUS 1988 hearing recommended remand and eventual dismissal), illustrate limits of reparations in addressing structural anxieties.

### Quantitative Comparison of Reparations Magnitudes

| Program | Total USD (cumulative) | Years active | Beneficiaries (approx.) | Per-capita approx. |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Germany — Holocaust | $86.8 billion | 1952–present | >500,000 direct + Israel | Variable (pensions scaled to suffering category; ~$1.6 billion/yr post-2018) |
| Germany — bilateral | DM 971 million (~$496 M) | 1959–closed | millions indirectly | Mass-distributed by home govts |
| U.S. — Japanese-American | ~$1.6+ billion | 1990–1998 | 82,219 + 145 Latin Americans | $20,000 (fixed per capita) |
| U.S. — Public Education Fund | $50 million authorized | 1990s–2000s | Public at large | N/A |

The contrast is striking: Germany's per-incident outlay was small in early years but ongoing for seven decades, whereas the U.S. response was a one-time closure after a 40-year delay. Total absolute spending differs by approximately two orders of magnitude.

---

## IV. Lustration in Post-Communist Eastern Europe

**Structure.** Lustration laws remove or screen persons associated with prior nondemocratic regimes from public office. According to Horne and Levi, countries clustered around three archetypes: *dismissal* (Czech Republic, Albania, Bulgaria, the former GDR); *exposure* (Hungary); and *confession* (Poland, partially Romania). Each model carries distinctive symbolic content and produces different attitudinal outcomes (Horne, *Lustration Systems and Trust*, *J. Pol.* 69:6; *Lustration Systems and Trust: Evidence from Survey Experiments in the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Poland*, UChicago Journals).

**Magnitude.** Czech Act No. 451/1991 screened roughly 700,000 individuals (only ~5% had formal records of collaboration; many cases were declined due to insufficient evidence). Poland's initial 1997 Act screened candidates for top posts only; later programs (2006, 2007) expanded to academics, journalists, and "positions of public trust." For Romania, the 2006 legislation published security-service files.

**Evaluation.**
- *Victims:* Most lustration schemes focused on perpetrators and beneficiaries, not on victims. Where victims of communist persecution were concerned, restitution occurred via separate national pension and rehabilitation laws. There is limited empirical evidence lustration provided direct reparative benefit.
- *Democratic transition:* Hough (*Late lustration programmes in Romania and Poland*) finds that late lustration was packaged with anti-corruption and judicial reform and "support[ed] democratic transitions." Horne's regression-based study of nine CEE countries shows that lustration "consistently and positively contributes to citizen trust in public institutions" controlling for growth, democratization, and corruption (*Assessing the Impact of Lustration*). However, lustration had "an indirect and diluted impact on trust in national government." Hanley and Hoschschild ("Lustration Matters") find that extensive lustration is associated with **~30% higher levels of democracy** (cross-country panel, 1996–2011), and that "lustration is effective in lowering corruption" with a high correlation (r = 0.75) between lustration index and Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI) in post-communist states. Survey experiments (Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland) found that **dismissal** and **confession** increase trust in government and tainted officials, while **exposure** (publishing names without removing them) *decreases* trust in tainted officials. **For complete effects on trust, the magnitudes vary and require context-specific interpretation.**
- *Non-recurrence:* Where lustration was most coercive (Czech "Big Bang"), it was most effective at deterring former collaborators from reentering state administration — but threatened rule-of-law norms and was criticized by the European Court of Human Rights (e.g., *Sovat v. Czech Republic*, *Chmelir v. Czech Republic*). Where lustration was symbolic (Poland), it generated less public cleansing and more democratic trust — but allowed some collaborators to retain influence.

---

## V. Comparative Synthesis

### A. Which Mechanism Serves Victims Best?

Survey research consistently finds that victims' preferences are heterogeneous. David & Choi (2009, *Political Psychology*, "Getting Even or Getting Equal?") survey former political prisoners in the Czech Republic and show that financial compensation, social acknowledgement, punishment, and forgiveness *each independently reduce* victims' retributive desires. African context survey research (Mueller-Hilty et al., "Retributive or reparative justice? Explaining post-conflict preferences in Kenya," *Journal of Peace Research* 2022) finds that **direct exposure to mass violence leads to greater preference for retributive prosecution over reparations**, but powerful ethnic co-membership (e.g., Kikuyu or Kalenjin) shifts preference toward reparations. The implication is that no single mechanism satisfies all victims; the most legitimate approach combines retributive, restorative, and reparative elements.

- TRC approach is strongest where victims primarily seek *truth-telling* and public acknowledgment.
- Prosecutorial tribunals are strongest where victims seek *validation of full criminal accountability*; their weakness is often geographic and temporal distance (Hague-based ICTY vs. local victims).
- Reparations are strongest where physical/material losses dominate (loss of property, capacity to work).
- Lustration is weakest as a victim-centered measure; its primary client is the political system.

### B. Which Best Enables Democratic Transitions?

Combining the empirical literature:
1. **Prosecutorial tribunals** (ICTY, ICC) produce durable rule-of-law infrastructure — the ICTY established JCE and the ICTR built post-genocide jurisprudence — and this is captured in international law as a permanent asset *if* domestic courts can absorb the residue (Bosnia's War Crimes Chamber, Croatia's specialized panels). However, when applied during fluid political transitions they can impede negotiated peace (ICC Kenya situation; ICC DRC, post-2009 Lubanga conviction followed by regional destabilization).
2. **Lustration** appears most directly linked to measurable democratic consolidation in post-communist settings (Horne; Hanley & Hoschschild).
3. **TRCs** produce immediate de-escalation but leave structural issues unaddressed; long-term democratization depends on whether reparations, judicial reform, and institutional change follow (TRC Canada: stalled at 13 actions in 2023 suggests limited automatic momentum).
4. **Reparations** allow re-integration into international society (Germany) without structural rupture; their democratic transition effect is contingent on accompanying commitments.

### C. Which Best Prevents Recurrence?

This is where the evidence is weakest and claims must be tempered. None of the four mechanisms has been empirically demonstrated to prevent recurrence on its own; what the empirical record suggests is that prevention requires a **comprehensive package** combining:
1. Truth documentation (combats denial — ICTY's record on Srebrenica is the archetype);
2. Criminal accountability of the top stratum (generates deterrence for current officeholders);
3. Institutional reform/vetting (the direct mechanism against re-infiltration by the old network);
4. Reparations (legitimizes the transition and addresses material grievances);
5. Education and memorialization (inter-generational).

Single-mechanism cases show recurring violence: South Africa (Marikana 2012, violent political-party dynamics); Darfur (renewed civil war 2023–). Mixed cases show better outcomes: Germany's fifty-year integration; Czech Republic's higher democracy scores relative to Russia (where no lustration, sustained high corruption — Hanley & Hoschschild).

---

## VI. Conclusions and Recommendations

1. **No single mechanism is sufficient.** The strongest cases for each single mechanism still exhibit major gaps (see §III, IV failures). The OHCHR guidance is right: transitional justice is "an enabler for prevention of conflict and serious violations, for sustaining peace, for accountability and the rule of law, for social cohesion, societal healing and reconciliation, and for sustainable development" (Guidance Note 2023). Mechanisms are complements, not substitutes.
2. **Truth and accountability must precede reconciliation goals.** The conviction of Mladić, Karadžić, and others was the "ultimate validation" of the ICTY's existence (ICTY Prosecutor, 12 May 2017 statement). Without accountability, truth commissions risk being perceived as the state's bargaining chip (a common reading of the South African TRC's amnesty decisions, with 5,392 refusals against 849 grants).
3. **Reparations should be calibrated to past atrocity and present capacity.** Germany's $86.8 billion reflects a multi-decade, multi-tier scheme tied to social policy; the U.S. $1.6 billion was a one-time remedial gesture. Both can be models depending on context, but neither satisfies victims by money alone.
4. **Lustration must be legal.** *Sovat v. Czech Republic* established that lustration laws are subject to ECHR proportionality review; the dismissal archetype is the most legally vulnerable but empirically the most deterrent. Hybrid models (confession or "purge plus acknowledgement") balance rule of law with public cleansing.
5. **For victims, surveys confirm plurality.** The David & Choi findings and the Kenyan evidence both suggest that retributive, restorative, and reparative measures serve **different** psychological and material needs. A victim-centered design must include all three (ICTJ, *Transforming Social Relations*, 2024: "restorative justice is at the center of transitional justice … the limitations of retributive systems for dealing with domestic crimes").
6. **Democratic consolidation is conditional and slow.** Outside Germany, longitudinal evidence suggests transitional-justice effects on democracy and trust take decades to materialize (Tandfonline, "Lustration Matters"). Unrealistic timelines damage legitimacy (Canada's TRC: 58-year projection; Sadc South Africa Twenty-year retrospective).
7. **Prevention of recurrence is the weakest empirically supported criterion.** Comprehensive packages produce the best results in preventing recurrence; single mechanisms rarely do.

### Final Verdict by Criterion

| Criterion | Best single mechanism | Best blended model | Caveat |
|---|---|---|---|
| Service to victims | Truth commissions (reparative + restorative dimension) | Holistic: prosecution + TRC + reparations + vetting | Victim preferences are heterogeneous |
| Democratic transition | Lustration (CEE empirics) + Germany-style reparations | Combined | Effects lagged; dependent on political/economic context |
| Prevention of recurrence | No single winner; ICTY + lustration + reparations + memorialization | Comprehensive package with all four pillars | Little rigorous evidence of pure prevention; correlation strong in Hungary and not strong in DPRK-like contexts |

The implication for policy is that the question "which approach is best?" is mis-framed. **A comprehensive framework that integrates the four pillars — truth, justice, reparations, guarantees of non-recurrence — and adopts a victim-centered, gender-responsive, context-specific design (OHCHR 2023) outperforms any single instrument.** Within such a framework, prosecutions of the top stratum (where feasible), truth commissions that drive systemic reform, lustration executed under rule-of-law constraints, sustained reparations, and education/memorialization combine to build durable democratic peace.
