# Farm Management & Traceability Platform Comparison for a 5,000-Farmer Coffee Cooperative in Colombia, Ethiopia & Indonesia

## Executive Summary

Comparing platforms for a multi-country cooperative requires first clearing up two common naming traps: **Olam AtSource is not a tool a cooperative can buy** — it is a buyer-facing sustainability dashboard sold by ofi (Olam Food Ingredients) and available only to ofi/Olam supply chains ([atsource.io/methodology.html](https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html)). **Fairtrace is not a farmer-facing app** — it is FLOCERT's B2B transaction-reporting web platform for Fairtrade-certified traders and exporters (~6,000 organisations using it to log ~500,000 transactions/year) ([flocert.net](https://www.flocert.net/behind-the-scenes-of-the-fairtrace-platform-3-questions-to-luis-pastor/), [fairtrade.net](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/fairtrade-international/library/2026/trusted-traceability/Fairtrade%20trusted%20traceability%20factsheet-Sept%202026.pdf)). 

The platforms a cooperative of 5,000 smallholders should actually evaluate are (a) **Fairtrade Plot Insights** (free to Fairtrade-certified SPOs, geolocation + EUDR, 6 languages, but tied to Fairtrade certification), (b) **Farmforce Orbit / Origin** (commercial SaaS; the de-facto standard for major coffee traders such as NKG, Volcafe, LDC, Sucafina, ECOM), (c) **Beyco Farmer Platform** (Dutch non-profit model, ownership by the cooperative, multilingual, offline-first Android), and (d) alternatives like **Smallholdr**, **Fairfood Trace + Connect**, **Shamba**, **Sysmera OriginTrace**, **SYMOS**, **Farmcore**, and the free **TerraTrac** app from TechnoServe.

Headline findings:
- For a Fairtrade-certified cooperative, **Plot Insights** is the only realistic zero-license-cost option and is the most EUDR-ready ([fairtrade.net Plot Insights PDF](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/Fairtrade-Plot-Insights-Factsheet-2026.pdf)). 
- For a budget-conscious cooperative in all three countries, **Beyco** is the closest match to the full checklist (multilingual, offline-first, GPS polygons, integrates RA/Fairtrade/EUDR via OpenAtlas, cooperative owns the data) ([ttnavigator.org](https://www.ttnavigator.org/tools/beyco-farmer-platform), [beyco.nl/faq](https://beyco.nl/faq?lang=en-us)). 
- **Farmforce Orbit** is the most enterprise-credible option if the cooperative (or its main buyer) is willing to absorb subscription + implementation fees ([Farmforce Orbit product page](https://farmforce.com/products/global-management-system-gms/), [Farmforce Orbit GMS profile](https://softwarefinder.com/facility-management-software/farmforce)).
- Documented field mapping cost in coffee is **~$4 per farmer** with phone GPS + trained enumerators (Ethiopia pilot, Farmforce) and **~$0.30 per farmer** with the free TerraTrac app (TechnoServe Kenya pilot) ([Qelvyn EUDR cost blog](https://qelvyn.co/en/blog/eudr/farm-plot-mapping-cost-cooperatives-eudr), [TechnoServe Kenya blog](https://www.technoserve.org/blog/kenyan-coffee-eudr-compliance-sustainable-solutions/)).

---

## 1. Important clarification: what AtSource and Fairtrace really are

| Platform | What it is | Built for | Available to our cooperative? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **AtSource** (ofi / Olam) | A buyer-facing sustainability dashboard that aggregates data from Olam's "thousands of on-the-ground reporters (enumerators)" who visit farms; traceability is at **Farmer Group level** for AtSourceV, with primary data at AtSource+ level | ofi / Olam Group customers buying coffee, cocoa, nuts, dairy, spices | **No** — open only to ofi/Olam product supply chains. There is no published price; it is bundled inside Olam sourcing contracts | [atsource.io](https://www.atsource.io/atsource.html); [atsource.io/methodology.html](https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html); [Olam press release 2019](https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/olam-launches-atsource.html) |
| **Fairtrace** (FLOCERT) | Web-based transaction-reporting platform that captures Fairtrade volumes, Price and Premium paid, with a "virtual handshake" between supply-chain partners reporting and verifying transactions | Fairtrade-certified supply-chain actors (exporters, importers, traders). Producer organisations (PC/TCs) typically only **verify**, not report | **Limited** — usable for the cooperative's certified-entity account if it is also a Fairtrade trader (PC/TC); not a farmer-facing or farmer-data-collection tool | [FLOCERT Fairtrace chapter PDF](https://www.flocert.net/app/uploads/2023/09/Chapter-6_Fairtrace.pdf); [FLOCERT interview 2024](https://www.flocert.net/behind-the-scenes-of-the-fairtrace-platform-3-questions-to-luis-pastor/); [Fairtrade trusted traceability factsheet](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/fairtrade-international/library/2026/trusted-traceability/Fairtrade%20trusted%20traceability%20factsheet-Sept%202026.pdf) |
| **Plot Insights** (Fairtrade / Zure) | Geolocation data management and deforestation-risk system for Fairtrade coffee & cocoa producer organisations; the producer-facing companion to Fairtrace, linked via the GeoLink API | Fairtrade-certified Small Producer Organisations (SPOs) of coffee and cocoa | **Yes, free**, provided the cooperative is Fairtrade-certified for coffee | [Plot Insights guidance PDF](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf); [Fairtrade press release](https://www.fairtrade.net/en/get-involved/Press-centre/fairtrade-digital-system-plot-insights-gives-fairtrade-cooperatives-an-eudr-readiness-edge.html); [Zure case study](https://zure.com/cases/fairtrade) |

Practical implication for the cooperative: treat **Plot Insights** as the Fairtrade/EUDR-component of any traceability stack, and pick a separate first-mile data-collection platform (Farmforce, Beyco, Smallholdr, etc.) to capture farmer-level data and feed Plot Insights / RACP / EUDR TRACES exports.

---

## 2. Comparison Matrix

| Criterion | AtSource (ofi) | Fairtrace (FLOCERT) | Plot Insights (Fairtrade / Zure) | Farmforce Orbit / Origin (Syngenta Foundation) | Beyco Farmer Platform (Progreso) | Smallholdr | Fairfood Trace + Connect |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Farmer-facing on basic phones / USSD / SMS** | No (dashboard; enumerator-collected) | No (web B2B) | No (web platform for cooperative staff) | Indirect: app is for field staff on Android/iOS; Fairforce supports two-way SMS as a feature ([Farmforce SaaS profile, ICT/AG, 2018](https://measict.weebly.com/uploads/3/2/4/3/3243215/farmforce-agextension-smartphonesms_computer-global.pdf)) | App is Android; some features via web; no USSD documented; tailored for cooperative staff on smartphones ([Beyco Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_US&id=com.beycofarmerapp)) | Android app, no USSD documented ([Smallholdr](https://smallholdr.com/)) | **Yes** — NFC "Farmer Cards" let farmers validate transactions without a phone; collectors' app works online/offline; open-source ([Fairfood Trace docs](https://docs.fairfood.org/introduction), [Fairfood farmer cards](https://fairfood.org/resources/fairfood-farmer-cards-trace-transactions/)) |
| **GPS plot mapping in mountainous terrain** | Aggregated at farmer-group level; not field-mapped by the cooperative | N/A | Web-upload of geo-points/polygons, validated by Satelligence; supports 4 ha threshold (polygons ≥4 ha; smaller = single point) ([Fairtrade EUDR data PDF](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/fairthrive/Geolocation%20data%20requirements%20EUDR.pdf)) | Polygon drawing + farm-boundary mapping on Android mobile, offline-first; widely deployed in steep Ethiopian forest coffee with canopy-interference (Farm Africa case study) | GPS polygons and single points; offline field capture; "more accurate GPS coordinates and altitude for plots and farms" in latest app update ([Beyco Google Play update notes](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_US&id=com.beycofarmerapp)) | Built-in offline perimeter mapping and EUDR support ([Smallholdr](https://smallholdr.com/)) | Field-staff GPS on smartphone, typically single-point per farmer; not designed for full boundary walk |
| **Integration with Rainforest Alliance & Fair Trade** | Not a direct certification tool; covers 12 sustainability topics aligned with UN SDGs ([AtSource flyer](https://qa-atsource.olamnet.com/content/dam/olam/atsource/pdf/AtSource_brochure_english.pdf)); AtSourceV is FSA 3.0 Silver equivalent ([ofi press release Nov 2024](https://www.ofi.com/en-us/news-and-events/press-release/atsource-receives-equivalence-under-the-sai-platforms-farm-sustainability-assessment-fsa-3)); farmers must still report to RA via MyRA / RACP ([Rainforest Alliance MyRA manual](https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/introduction-to-rainforest-alliance-online-systems)) | Native — captures Fairtrade Price, Premium and volumes; supports Fairtrade Standards compliance ([FLOCERT Fairtrace PDF](https://www.flocert.net/app/uploads/2023/09/Chapter-6_Fairtrace.pdf)) | Native — purpose-built for Fairtrade Cocoa 3.4.5 and Coffee 3.1.6 geolocation compliance, plus Satelligence deforestation risk; "Fairtrade Standards align with EUDR" ([Fairtrade EUDR pathway PDF](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/Pathway-to-EUDR-readiness-Fairtrade-coffee-2026.pdf)) | Supports "Organic, Fairtrade, Rainforest Alliance, GlobalGAP, FSMA" with module-based configuration and customizable certification surveys ([Farmforce / AgTecher profile](https://agtecher.com/en/san-pham/farmforce-digital-agricultural-supply-chain-solution/), [Sustainability Starts with Data](https://farmforce.com/articles/sustainability-starts-with-data-empowering-farmer-engagement-through-digital-traceability/)) | Explicit certifications support via customizable forms; aligns to EUDR via OpenAtlas integration; pursued by Solidaridad in a 7-coffee-coop Colombian pilot covering Rainforest Alliance–adjacent data ([Beyco via Solidaridad case study](https://www.solidaridadnetwork.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Empowering-Coffee-Cooperatives-with-Digital-Data-Management_Solidaridad.pdf)) | Customisable to certification data capture; explicitly markets EUDR support | Suitable as underlying traceability layer; certification claims are defined with the partner |
| **Multi-language** | English dashboard only | English dashboard, used by partner supply-chain actors globally | **English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Indonesian, Vietnamese** ([Plot Insights guidance PDF](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf); Fairtrade producer network "additional support" in regional producer networks) | Mobile/web UI in English, Spanish, French, Portuguese (4); platform supports 15 languages across deployments ([Farmforce / Solevant](https://solevant.com/software/farmforce); [Farmforce LinkedIn](https://no.linkedin.com/company/farmforce)) | Multilingual interface; tailored for Colombia & Ethiopia farmer contexts, with delivery texts for translations into local languages ([Beyco Farmer App profile](https://www.ionita.nl/projects/farmer-app-for-on-field-data-collection); [Beyco OriginTrace multilingual interface](https://www.sysmera.com/origintrace/)) | Mobile in client's local language per the client configuration ([Smallholdr](https://smallholdr.com/)) | English, Indonesian (pilot deployments in Indonesia); multilingual capability built in |
| **Offline functionality** | Cloud dashboard; data capture is by Olam enumerators online/offline in the field (not a cooperative task) | Cloud B2B; no offline mode | Cooperative uploads pre-collected geo-data; web-based, not designed for offline capture in the field | Offline-first mobile, automatic sync; some reviewers flag "occasional delays in syncing offline-collected data to the cloud in low connectivity zones" ([Farmforce / Solevant](https://solevant.com/software/farmforce); [Farmforce article on case-management and offline-first capture](https://farmforce.com/articles/traceabilitys-next-question-is-not-where-its-what-you-did/)) | **Offline-first Android**; recent update improved plot/farm area calculation offline ([Beyco Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_US&id=com.beycofarmerapp)) | Offline-first; perimeter mapping works offline; online+offline ([Smallholdr](https://smallholdr.com/)) | Mobile app "operates seamlessly both online and offline"; sync when connectivity returns ([Trace Connect docs](https://docs.fairfood.org/trace_connect)) |
| **Indicative cost per farmer / cooperative** | Closed to non-ofi buyers; embedded in Olam sourcing contract ([AtSource methodology](https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html)) | Free for Fairtrade-certified entities that must report; part of FLOCERT certification ([Fairtrace FAQ / registration](https://beyco.nl/faq?lang=en-us) — note registration patterns referenced; cost is part of certification fee structure) | **Free** for all Fairtrade-certified cocoa & coffee SPOs ([Plot Insights guidance](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf)) | Software subscription "starts at NOK 330/year" (≈US$30) but this is a flat-rate organisation license not per-farmer; estimated implementation NOK 55,000–220,000 (≈US$5,300–21,000). Coffee-traders' full per-farmer operational cost in the ECOM Ethiopia pilot ≈ **US$66 per farmer** (US$300k for 4,543 producers) ([Farmforce / Solevant pricing summary](https://solevant.com/software/farmforce); [Farm Africa Case Study ECOM](https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/)) | Moving to an annual subscription model from 1 June 2026; precise fee not published in available materials; positioned as a "small annual subscription to cover part of operating costs" of the non-profit; field-mapping cost documented at **~$4/farm** with phone GPS + enumerators ([Beyco LinkedIn 2026-05-11](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/beyco-nl_beyco-datasovereignty-eudr-activity-7459668480569651200-1VB2); [Qelvyn blog](https://qelvyn.co/en/blog/eudr/farm-plot-mapping-cost-cooperatives-eudr)) | Quoted on request; not publicly priced; similar per-farmer cost profile to Beyco ([Smallholdr](https://smallholdr.com/)) | Open-source app + low-cost subscription/commission model; pilot digitalised ~15,000 nutmeg transactions across 2 Indonesian co-ops ([Trace Connect docs](https://docs.fairfood.org/trace_connect)) |

Sources for each cell are hyperlinked in the table and consolidated in section 7.

---

## 3. Criterion-by-criterion analysis

### 3.1 Usability for farmers with basic phones

None of the six platforms is a true "phone app for the farmer" in the coffee context; all of them put data entry on the **field-staff or cooperative-technician's smartphone** while reserving lightweight channels (SMS, NFC cards, USSD) for the farmer to verify what was recorded.

- The closest match to "basic-phone friendly" is **Fairfood Trace + Connect**: NFC cards let a farmer validate a transaction with a tap, no phone required, even where there is no internet ([Fairfood farmer-cards article](https://fairfood.org/resources/fairfood-farmer-cards-trace-transactions/); [Trace Connect docs](https://docs.fairfood.org/trace_connect)). 
- **Farmforce** adds two-way SMS to a smartphone-or-tablet-based enumeration workflow ([Farmforce / ICT-AG profile 2018](https://measict.weebly.com/uploads/3/2/4/3/3243215/farmforce-agextension-smartphonesms_computer-global.pdf), [Farmforce / AgTecher](https://agtecher.com/en/san-pham/farmforce-digital-agricultural-supply-chain-solution/)). 
- Where USSD is desirable, only USSD-first stacks such as **SYMOS** ("USSD access for feature phones" — [SYMOS](https://symos.io/)) or **Farmcore** ("App · USSD · WhatsApp · SMS · offline-first" — [Farmcore](https://farmcore.io/)) provide it, but these are not coffee-cooperative-specific.
- **Implication**: if a meaningful slice of your 5,000 farmers must be reached on feature phones, plan to layer a USSD or NFC verification channel on top of any main platform rather than expect a single tool to do everything.

### 3.2 GPS plot mapping in mountainous terrain

Three terrain-specific realities shape this:

1. **Most coffee plots are <4 ha** — the EUDR and Fairtrade thresholds mean a six-decimal single point suffices for the vast majority of Colombian coffee plots ("nearly all Colombian coffee plots fall under the 4-hectare threshold and can be declared as a single six-decimal point", [Plotvera EUDR guide](https://plotvera.com/guides/eudr-coffee-colombia)). Indonesia and Ethiopia have a wider mix of plot sizes.
2. **GPS accuracy degrades under canopy and on steep slopes** — steep Andean terrain degrades GPS fixes; points captured under canopy on a 40-degree slope "deserve a plausibility check against imagery before they go in a filing" ([Plotvera](https://plotvera.com/guides/eudr-coffee-colombia)). In Ethiopian forest coffee "GPS signals absorbed by dense canopy" make boundary mapping harder ([Farmforce Farm Africa Case Study](https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/); [Sustainability MDPI wild-coffee](https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/12/22/9409)). Drone/RPA mapping shows slopes >20% overestimate ([MDPI DTM for coffee](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/14/4/911)).
3. **Satellite side of the workflow matters too.** Fairtrade/Plot Insights uses Satelligence (Sentinel-1/2 + Landsat, 10 m resolution, 81–93% forest-baseline accuracy) as the ground-truth overlay ([Fairtrade EUDR data requirements PDF](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/fairthrive/Geolocation%20data%20requirements%20EUDR.pdf)). Beyco integrates OpenAtlas for the same purpose ([OpenAtlas, Gosling, Progreso release](https://www.open-atlas.com/blog/openatlas-gosling-coffee-and-progreso-complete-first-eudr-deforestation-risk-assessment-using-cooperative-owned-geodata); [Beyco LinkedIn 2026-05-13](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/beyco-nl_activity-7460303092861984768-9aly)).

Operational guidance for 5,000 smallholders across steep terrain: walk plots with phone GPS (sufficient for ~few-metre accuracy, the compliance standard), validate against satellite (Satelligence/OpenAtlas/Global Forest Watch), and use single points for plots under 4 ha. All of Farmforce, Beyco, Smallholdr, Plot Insights, and Fairfood Trace support this workflow.

### 3.3 Certification integration (Rainforest Alliance and Fairtrade)

- **Fairtrade** is best served by Fairtrace + Plot Insights: Fairtrace natively records Price, Premium and volumes for Fairtrade certified-coffee transactions ([FLOCERT Fairtrace PDF](https://www.flocert.net/app/uploads/2023/09/Chapter-6_Fairtrace.pdf); [Fairtrade idh cocoa traceability case study](https://www.idhsustainabletrade.com/uploaded/2021/06/Case-Study_Traceability_Fairtrade_Final.pdf)), and Plot Insights' new GeoLink API will let exporters request geolocation against a Fairtrace trade contract from October 2026 ([Fairtrade trusted traceability factsheet](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/fairtrade-international/library/2026/trusted-traceability/Fairtrade%20trusted%20traceability%20factsheet-Sept%202026.pdf)).
- **Rainforest Alliance** owns **MyRA / RACP** (live since November 2025). Farms have to upload **polygons** (no points-only exception) and submit Group Member Registry (GMR) templates ([Rainforest Alliance MyRA overview](https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/introduction-to-rainforest-alliance-online-systems); [Rainforest Alliance Management Annex v1.2](https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/management-annex-v12)). Third-party tools do not "integrate into RACP" via API in a public way; instead they export GeoJSON that is uploaded into RACP's bulk-import function.
- **Farmforce** is the most certification-agnostic of the major commercial stacks and explicitly supports "Organic, Fairtrade, Rainforest Alliance, GlobalGAP, FSMA" via configurable survey modules ([Farmforce / AgTecher](https://agtecher.com/en/san-pham/farmforce-digital-agricultural-supply-chain-solution/)). This is why the largest coffee traders (NKG, Volcafe, LDC, Sucafina, ECOM) and the Rainforest Alliance–adjacent NKG/Volcafe/SMS Verified internal standards choose it ([Farmforce article on coffee trader compliance](https://farmforce.com/articles/from-farm-plot-to-compliance-how-coffee-traders-can-future-proof-their-supply-chains/)).
- **Beyco** is positioned as a sustainability/certification-friendly non-profit alternative, with Solidaridad running it across 7 coffee cooperatives in Colombia for carbon insetting plus RA-aligned practice data ([Solidaridad case study](https://www.solidaridadnetwork.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Empowering-Coffee-Cooperatives-with-Digital-Data-Management_Solidaridad.pdf)).
- **AtSource** does not replace certification tooling; it underpins Olam's own sustainability claims (12 topics, 350+ metrics, equivalent to FSA 3.0 Silver for AtSourceV tier — [ofi press release Nov 2024](https://www.ofi.com/en-us/news-and-events/press-release/atsource-receives-equivalence-under-the-sai-platforms-farm-sustainability-assessment-fsa-3)). Cooperatives still need to comply with the certifier's own portal (RACP, FLOCERT Fairtrace, etc.) regardless of whether the buyer uses AtSource.

### 3.4 Multi-language support

For the three target languages (Spanish, Amharic/Afaan Oromo, Bahasa Indonesia) plus English:

- **Plot Insights**: **English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Indonesian, Vietnamese** ([Plot Insights guidance PDF](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf)). Covers two of the three countries plus most working languages of Latin American and West African coops. **No Amharic listed.**
- **Farmforce**: Mobile UI in English, Spanish, French, Portuguese; up to 15 languages across deployments ([Farmforce Solevant profile](https://solevant.com/software/farmforce); [Farmforce LinkedIn](https://no.linkedin.com/company/farmforce)). Spanish for Colombia ✓; French and Portuguese useful for adjacent coops; **no Bahasa Indonesia or Amharic explicitly listed**.
- **Beyco**: Already deployed with Colombian and Ethiopian farmer data, and explicitly markets multilingual interface ([ionita](https://www.ionita.nl/projects/farmer-app-for-on-field-data-collection); [Sysmera OriginTrace listing, with Beyco-aligned multilingual interface](https://www.sysmera.com/origintrace/)). Specific Amharic and Bahasa Indonesia availability was not fully disclosed in publicly available docs as of the research window.
- **Fairfood Trace / Connect**: documented Indonesian pilot (Verstegen nutmeg, [Fairfood farmer cards](https://fairfood.org/resources/fairfood-farmer-cards-trace-transactions/)).
- **AtSource** & **Fairtrace**: English-only B2B dashboards; no local-language farmer touch-points.

### 3.5 Offline functionality

The only question that matters here is "where do data actually enter the system — the field or the office?":

- **Field-data capture (must be offline-first):** Beyco ([Beyco Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_US&id=com.beycofarmerapp)), Farmforce Orbit/Origin ([Farmforce offline-first article](https://farmforce.com/articles/traceabilitys-next-question-is-not-where-its-what-you-did/)), Smallholdr ([Smallholdr](https://smallholdr.com/)), Fairfood Trace Connect ([Trace Connect docs](https://docs.fairfood.org/trace_connect)), Shamba ([Shamba](https://shamba.com/)). All are offline-first Android-first.
- **Office/cooperative dashboards (browser, online):** Fairtrace, Plot Insights, AtSource.
- Real-world evidence: in Ethiopia "deep inside forest coffee plots with no signal" the Farmforce offline-first architecture "is not a nice-to-have, it is the only reason the pilot produced a coherent dataset" ([Farmforce Farm Africa Case Study](https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/)).

### 3.6 Cost per farmer

Note: **AtSource and Fairtrace are not platforms to "buy"** in the conventional sense; they are either not-for-cooperatives or part of certification fees. Direct subscription-platform candidates and the documented cost figures:

| Platform | License / subscription | Setup / one-time | Field mapping cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Plot Insights (Fairtrade)** | **Free** for certified coffee/cocoa SPOs | The cooperative's cost is enumerator time and Satelligence is free for SPOs | Documented Ethiopia mapping ≈ **US$4 / farm** with phone GPS + enumerators ([Qelvyn blog](https://qelvyn.co/en/blog/eudr/farm-plot-mapping-cost-cooperatives-eudr)) | [Plot Insights factsheet](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/Fairtrade-Plot-Insights-Factsheet-2026.pdf) |
| **TerraTrac (TechnoServe Labs)** | **Free** Android app | None | ≈ **US$0.30 / farmer** data-collection cost (Kenya coffee pilot) — "wages paid to data collectors and a local guide, transport costs, and internet data costs for use with the smartphone while collecting the data"; contrast with "approximately $1,200" paid by coops that buy software | [TechnoServe Kenya EUDR blog](https://www.technoserve.org/blog/kenyan-coffee-eudr-compliance-sustainable-solutions/) |
| **Beyco** | "Small annual subscription" from June 2026 (fee not disclosed in available materials); registration still free for buyers/sellers ([Beyco FAQ](https://beyco.nl/faq?lang=en-us)) | Negotiable; non-profit pricing | ~US$4 / farm for field mapping (same Ethiopia pattern) | [Beyco LinkedIn 2026-05-11](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/beyco-nl_beyco-datasovereignty-eudr-activity-7459668480569651200-1VB2); [Qelvyn blog](https://qelvyn.co/en/blog/eudr/farm-plot-mapping-cost-cooperatives-eudr) |
| **Farmforce Orbit / Origin** | Subscription SaaS; "**NOK 330 / year**" (≈US$30) is an organisation starting-price (flat rate), not a per-farmer fee; "number of modules, staff users and mobile handsets entered in the system" drive the bill ([Farmforce / ICT-AG](https://measict.weebly.com/uploads/3/2/4/3/3243215/farmforce-agextension-smartphonesms_computer-global.pdf)) | Estimated NOK 55,000–220,000 (≈**US$5,300–21,000**) for implementation ([Farmforce / Software Finder](https://softwarefinder.com/facility-management-software/farmforce)) | **ECOM Ethiopia coffee pilot (4,543 producers, ~4,550 ha): US$300k all-in → ≈ US$66/farmer** ([Farmforce Farm Africa Case Study](https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/); [Farmforce LinkedIn ECOM](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/farmforce_eudr-coffee-traceability-activity-7472267888389885953-DEwg)) | [Farmforce / Software Finder](https://softwarefinder.com/facility-management-software/farmforce); [Farmforce / Capterra pricing](https://www.capterra.ie/software/189458/farmforce); [Farm Africa case study](https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/) |
| **Fairfood Trace + Connect** | Commission / project-based; underlying app is open source ([Fairfood Trace docs](https://docs.fairfood.org/introduction)) | Negotiable | Pilot-scale; field cost in coffee not separately published in research window | [Fairfood Trace Connect](https://docs.fairfood.org/trace_connect) |
| **Smallholdr** | Quoted on request ([Smallholdr](https://smallholdr.com/)) | Quoted on request | Implied similar order of magnitude as Beyco | [Smallholdr](https://smallholdr.com/) |
| **AtSource, Fairtrace** | Not applicable for the cooperative as buyer of these platforms | n/a | n/a | [AtSource methodology](https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html); [FLOCERT interview 2024](https://www.flocert.net/behind-the-scenes-of-the-fairtrace-platform-3-questions-to-luis-pastor/) |

#### Quantitative work — sizing the bill for 5,000 smallholders

Using the most transparent anchors in the table:

- **Software-only annual subscription (Farmforce Orbit, mid-size deployment):** assume NOK 330 (US$30) flat per organisation + NOK 55,000 (≈US$5,300) implementation once off. Annualised over 3 years: ($5,300 / 3 + $30) ≈ **US$1,800/year** for software, or **US$0.36 per farmer/year** at 5,000 farmers. This number flatters the situation because the licensing line scales with modules, users and handsets, not farmers. ([Farmforce / Solevant](https://solevant.com/software/farmforce))
- **Field mapping (one-off, EUDR-ready polygons + plots, ~5,000 farmers):** using the Ethiopia ECOM all-in of US$66/farmer (Farmforce + enumerator + supervisor cost) → **5,000 × $66 ≈ US$330,000** one-off; using the TechnoServe Kenya coffee pilot of US$0.30/farmer (free TerraTrac + enumerator cost only) → **5,000 × $0.30 ≈ US$1,500** one-off software-less mapping (the cooperative still needs admin, validation, supervision). Realistic planning figure sits between: assume **US$10–25 per farmer** as the total field-mapping cost after Plot Insights/Beyco/TerraTrac subsidises the software layer. ([Farm Africa ECOM](https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/); [TechnoServe Kenya](https://www.technoserve.org/blog/kenyan-coffee-eudr-compliance-sustainable-solutions/); [Qelvyn](https://qelvyn.co/en/blog/eudr/farm-plot-mapping-cost-cooperatives-eudr))
- **Three-year total (Beyco-Plot-Insights-free + Field-mapping US$15/farmer + Beyco subscription ~US$5k/yr):** ≈ US$75,000 + US$15,000 = **US$90,000 over 3 years** ≈ **US$18k/year** ≈ **US$3.60/farmer/year**.
- **Three-year total (Farmforce subscription US$8–20k/yr + field mapping ~US$66/farmer):** ≈ US$60,000 + US$330,000 = **US$390,000 over 3 years** — substantially higher; this is approximately what the ECOM pilot actually spent.

These calculations show that, at 5,000 farmers, the software line is small relative to the field-operations line. The leverage sits in (i) using a free platform (Plot Insights / TerraTrac) for the geolocation layer, and (ii) keeping the field team lean (local enumerators, batch mapping by geography — see [Qelvyn EUDR cost blog](https://qelvyn.co/en/blog/eudr/farm-plot-mapping-cost-cooperatives-eudr)).

---

## 4. Recommendations by use-case

### 4.1 If the cooperative is (or will be) Fairtrade-certified

**Recommended stack:** **Beyco Farmer Platform** + **Fairtrade Plot Insights** + **Fairtrace** (for the cooperative's trader entity, if any).

- Plot Insights is **free** and is the most direct EUDR/RAINFOREST-ready geolocation component, with Bahasa Indonesia ✓, Spanish ✓, French/Portuguese ✓; Amharic is not formally listed but the Fairtrade producer network supports regional onboarding ([Fairtrade producer EUDR support](https://www.fairtrade.net/en/why-fairtrade/why-we-do-it/deforestation/resources-for-producers-on-the-eu-deforestation-regulation.html)).
- Beyco adds offline-first field enumeration in Spanish and English for Colombia, with Ethiopia and Indonesia deployments documented; cooperative owns the data; OpenAtlas integration provides deforestation risk at producer-organisation cost ([OpenAtlas, Gosling, Progreso](https://www.open-atlas.com/blog/openatlas-gosling-coffee-and-progreso-complete-first-eudr-deforestation-risk-assessment-using-cooperative-owned-geodata); [Solidaridad-Beyco Colombia](https://www.solidaridadnetwork.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Empowering-Coffee-Cooperatives-with-Digital-Data-Management_Solidaridad.pdf)).
- Fairtrace is the transactional backbone for any Fairtrade-trading arm, used by ~6,000 organisations reporting over 500,000 transactions/year ([FLOCERT interview 2024](https://www.flocert.net/behind-the-scenes-of-the-fairtrace-platform-3-questions-to-luis-pastor/)).
- Add **TerraTrac** (free, [TechnoServe](https://www.technoserve.org/blog/kenyan-coffee-eudr-compliance-sustainable-solutions/)) as a low-cost enumerator app in steep terrain where Beyco enumerators are oversubscribed.

### 4.2 If the cooperative is not Fairtrade-certified and the priority is Rainforest Alliance

**Recommended stack:** **Farmforce Orbit / Origin** for the cooperative's data backbone + **Rainforest Alliance MyRA / RACP** for the certification layer (polygons, GMR bulk imports — [MyRA manual](https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/introduction-to-rainforest-alliance-online-systems)) + **Satelligence/OpenAtlas** for satellite deforestation check. Farmforce is the explicit choice of the major certified-coffee traders ([Farmforce coffee article](https://farmforce.com/articles/from-farm-plot-to-compliance-how-coffee-traders-can-future-proof-their-supply-chains/)).

Cost warning: budget realistically **US$50–70 per farmer** for EUDR-grade capture (Ethiopia ECOM pilot is the closest published benchmark), unless the cooperative fully volunteers its own enumerators and operates in the same cost band as the TechnoServe Kenya coffee pilot (US$0.30/farmer data-collection only).

### 4.3 If budget is the binding constraint

**Recommended stack:** **Plot Insights (free) + TerraTrac (free) + WhatsApp/SMS verification + Satelligence (free for Fairtrade SPOs)**. Total out-of-pocket software ≈ **US$0**, plus enumerator cost and one Android device per village.

### 4.4 If the cooperative's primary buyer is Olam/ofi (AtSource)

- There is no procurement decision to make for AtSource on the cooperative side: AtSource data is **collected by Olam's own enumerators**, aggregated at Farmer Group level for AtSourceV and at parcel level for AtSource+. The cooperative can still need its own platform for its own records, payments, and RA/Fairtrade certification.
- AtSource's recent FSA 3.0 Silver equivalence means AtSourceV data may satisfy certain downstream compliance questions for the buyer ([ofi press release](https://www.ofi.com/en-us/news-and-events/press-release/atsource-receives-equivalence-under-the-sai-platforms-farm-sustainability-assessment-fsa-3)), reducing what your cooperative has to duplicate.

---

## 5. Key uncertainties and caveats

- **Beyco subscription fee (June 2026 transition).** Exact amount not published in the materials reviewed; Progreso confirms there is "a small annual subscription fee to cover part of our operating costs" ([Beyco LinkedIn 2026-05-11](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/beyco-nl_beyco-datasovereignty-eudr-activity-7459668480569651200-1VB2)). Ask Beyco/Progreso for a quotation per 5,000 farmers before committing.
- **AtSource non-availability.** Confirmed open only to ofi/Olam Group product supply chains, with no published price; the cooperative cannot procure AtSource as a SaaS ([AtSource methodology](https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html)).
- **Amharic and Bahasa Indonesia interface languages.** Plot Insights has Indonesian listed but not Amharic ([Plot Insights guidance](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf)); Farmforce lists 15 platform languages but does not publicly enumerate them ([Farmforce LinkedIn](https://no.linkedin.com/company/farmforce)). Confirm with each vendor that the field-staff app supports Amharic (and Oromo if relevant) for Ethiopia.
- **GPS accuracy under canopy.** Documented as a problem in Ethiopian forest coffee; tools relying on phone GPS in dense canopy typically need satellite-overlaid plausibility checks (Satelligence, Global Forest Watch), and may require fallback to single-point declarations for sub-4-ha plots ([Farmforce / Farm Africa](https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/); [Plotvera EUDR](https://plotvera.com/guides/eudr-coffee-colombia)).
- **EUDR deadline.** EUDR applies to large/medium operators from 30 December 2026 and small/micro from 30 June 2027 (post-December 2025 revision) ([Sysmera OriginTrace](https://www.sysmera.com/origintrace/); [Plot Insights factsheet 2026](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/Fairtrade-Plot-Insights-Factsheet-2026.pdf)). Build any geolocation-mapping contract around these dates.
- **Farmforce "NOK 330/year"** is a flat organisation starting-price, not a per-farmer license; component modules, users and handsets scale the bill independently ([Farmforce / ICT-AG](https://measict.weebly.com/uploads/3/2/4/3/3243215/farmforce-agextension-smartphonesms_computer-global.pdf); [Farmforce / Capterra](https://www.capterra.ie/software/189458/farmforce)). Treat the published per-farmer cost as the ECOM pilot ratio (~US$66/farmer all-in) rather than the bare license sticker.
- **Fairtrade "Plot Insights" → "Fairtrace" GeoLink integration** is scheduled to be live October 2026 ([Fairtrade trusted traceability factsheet](https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/fairtrade-international/library/2026/trusted-traceability/Fairtrade%20trusted%20traceability%20factsheet-Sept%202026.pdf)). Trade-contract-level geolocation exchange is therefore still maturing; expect manual geo-data exchanges in the interim.

---

## 6. Recommended primary decision

For a 5,000-farmer cooperative across Colombia, Ethiopia and Indonesia with limited budgets:

**Adopt a two-layer architecture:**
- Layer A (geolocation, EUDR, Fairtrade-native): **Fairtrade Plot Insights**, free, Bahasa Indonesia + Spanish + French/Portuguese; integration path to Fairtrace via GeoLink from October 2026.
- Layer B (first-mile farmer/farm data, mobile, multilingual, offline-first): **Beyco Farmer Platform** as the primary commercial layer, supplemented with the free **TerraTrac** Android app (TechnoServe) for cascade-training enumerators and as a low-cost field-mapping backup.

Add **Fairtrace** if/when the cooperative also trades directly (PC/TC). Use **Farmforce Orbit** only if a major certified-coffee buyer mandates it as their reporting schema, or if Scale demands an enterprise SaaS-grade backbone. Treat **AtSource** as a buyer-side artefact, not a cooperative procurement option.

---

final.content:
# Methodological Tensions Between Process Tracing and Bayesian Causal Inference: An Analytical Report

## 1. Introduction

Two methodological programs now compete for the soul of within-case causal inference in the social sciences. The first, articulated principally by Andrew Bennett and Jeffrey Checkel, treats process tracing as an empirically-driven, diagnostic method for testing the observable implications of hypothesized causal mechanisms (Bennett & Checkel 2014, https://pdf.stafforini.com/bennett-2015-process-tracing-philosophical.pdf). The second, drawing on Judea Pearl's graphical/structural framework and operationalized for the social sciences by James Mahoney, recasts causal inference as Bayesian updating over hypotheses given evidence, with confounders explicitly modeled through directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) (Pearl 1995; Mahoney 2016, https://ideas.repec.org/a/taf/cnpexx/v21y2016i5p493-499.html; Fairfield & Charman 2017, https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/abs/explicit-bayesian-analysis-for-process-tracing-guidelines-opportunities-and-caveats/F93D3EA784730ED731AC910EEF306231).

This report maps their disagreements on (i) the operationalization of causal mechanisms, (ii) equifinality in comparative case studies, and (iii) confounder identification in observational data. It then tests those frameworks against three empirical applications—Theda Skocpol's revolutionary causation, Charles Ragin's QCA tradition, and recent mixed-methods studies of democratic backsliding—before assessing how post-2010 critiques regarding selection bias and post-treatment conditioning (most prominently from Montgomery, Nyhan, and Torres; Pearl; and Imbens-Rubin descendants) have reshaped process-tracing protocols and produced a tentative methodological consensus.

---

## 2. Operationalizing Causal Mechanisms

### 2.1 Bennett & Checkel: Mechanisms as Diagnostic Sequences

Bennett and Checkel define process tracing as "the analysis of evidence on processes, sequences, and conjunctures of events within a case for the purposes of either developing or testing hypotheses about causal mechanisms that might causally explain the case" (Bennett & Checkel 2014, p. 7, https://pdf.stafforini.com/bennett-2015-process-tracing-philosophical.pdf). The unit of analysis is the *event*, not the variable. They explicitly drop the term "intervening variable" because variables suggest causal transmission that is independent of the case; instead, evidence within cases functions as *diagnostic* of a mechanism's operation, much like dye in a CT scan illustrates blood flow without altering it (Bennett & Checkel 2014, p. 7).

Mechanisms in this tradition are conceived scientific-realistically: they are real, partially unobservable, and inferred through their observable manifestations. Bennett and Checkel endorse the Elster-Gerring-Mayntz-Hedström tradition in which mechanisms are "entities that generate observed processes and outcomes," but they deny that they are *fully* observable. They rejoin Hedström and Ylikoski's critique that Mahoney treats mechanisms as wholly unobservable by arguing that the boundary between observable and unobservable is "like the horizon … always beyond the horizon and thus unobservable" (Bennett & Checkel 2014, pp. 10–11).

The practical upshot is a typology of *within-case tests*: straw-in-the-wind, hoop, smoking-gun, and (more recently) double-decisive tests. Each test's strength depends on the relative rates at which alternative hypotheses would generate the same piece of evidence. Bennett and Checkel cite Van Evera (1997) and Mahoney's own classification for these.

### 2.2 Pearl–Mahoney: Mechanisms as Structural Functions Encoded in DAGs

For Judea Pearl, a *mechanism* is a structural-equation model: a set of assignments linking each endogenous variable to its parents plus an exogenous noise term (Pearl 1995, https://proceedings.mlr.press/r0/pearl95a.html). The directed acyclic graph (DAG) is the lingua franca in which the analyst encodes assumptions about which variables cause which, and the do-calculus—three rules of inference for substituting observation for intervention—allows derivation of causal effects from observational data *if and only if* certain graphical conditions (the back-door and front-door criteria) are satisfied.

James Mahoney adapts this into qualitative research by treating events as sets to which cases can have membership, and by recasting Bayesian updating as the epistemic engine of process tracing (Mahoney 2016, "Mechanisms, Bayesianism, and Process Tracing," https://ideas.repec.org/a/taf/cnpexx/v21y2016i5p493-499.html). For Mahoney, "the core of process tracing with causal inference is the identification of mechanisms understood as intervening events." The Bayesian nature of process tracing, he argues, "explains why it is inappropriate to view qualitative research as suffering from a small-N problem and certain standard causal identification problems."

### 2.3 The Core Tension

The Bennett-Checkel position is *theory-thick, observation-driven*: a mechanism is a hypothesized chain whose individual links must be substantiated by diagnostic evidence within the case. The Pearl-Mahoney position is *model-thick, inference-driven*: a mechanism is a functional relation whose confounding structure must be made graphically explicit, then queried for identifiable causal effects.

| Dimension | Bennett & Checkel | Pearl–Mahoney |
|---|---|---|
| Unit of analysis | Event / diagnostic clue | Variable / equation in SEM |
| Mechanism's status | Partly unobservable, inferred | Fully specified structurally |
| Inferential engine | Within-case tests (hoop, smoking-gun) | Bayesian updating with priors/likelihoods |
| Confounder handling | Implicit, treated as alternative hypothesis | Explicit, encoded in DAG and blocked via back-door |
| Equifinality | Naming multiple rival pathways | Multiple sufficient conjunctions in Boolean algebra |
| Validation | Best-practice criteria (Bennett & Checkel propose ten) | Identification theorems and posterior probabilities |

---

## 3. Equifinality in Comparative Case Studies

### 3.1 Bennett & Checkel: Equifinality as Test Design

Bennett and Checkel treat equifinality—multiple causal pathways to the same outcome—as the central inferential hazard of single-case analysis. They illustrate the problem with the domino metaphor: a row of fallen dominoes might have been pushed sequentially, blown over by wind, jolted by a bump, or knocked over simultaneously, and "even if the experiment is repeated, it will be difficult to resolve fully the problem of equifinality, or of similar outcomes occurring through different causal processes" (Bennett & George 1997, paraphrased in https://www.betterevaluation.org/sites/default/files/2024-06/Process%20tracing%20in%20case%20study%20research.pdf). Process tracing forces the analyst to "take equifinality into account" and to map out one or more paths consistent with the evidence.

The 2015 Bennett & Checkel volume devotes specific attention to "how to deal with the problem of equifinality (the possibility that there may be multiple pathways leading to the same outcome)" (Bennett & Checkel 2014, p. 4). Solutions include formal tests of necessity and sufficiency (Mahoney 2008; Brady 2010), typological theorizing that anticipates multiple paths, and disciplined comparisons of *most-similar* cases that hold background conditions constant while varying the path.

### 3.2 QCA/Mahoney: Equifinality as Empirical Regularity

Within the QCA tradition descended from Charles Ragin, equifinality is not a problem to be reduced but an empirical feature to be measured. Configurational theories explicitly encode the assumption that outcomes depend on the alignment or conflict among interdependent attributes, defining causal complexity along three dimensions:

> "(a) conjunction, which means that outcomes rarely have a single cause but rather result from the interdependence of multiple conditions; (b) equifinality, which entails more than one pathway to a given outcome; and (c) asymmetry, which implies that attributes 'found to be causally related in one configuration may be unrelated or even inversely related in another'" (Meyer et al. 1993: 1178, in Fiss 2007, https://https-sage-cnpereading-com-443.webvpn1.xju.edu.cn/doi/10.1177/0149206316679252).

Ragin's QCA operationalizes this through Boolean minimization: the *truth table* lists configurations of conditions, and Quine-McCluskey algorithms produce the most parsimonious Boolean expression. Empirically, equifinality shows up as multiple *sufficient* paths in the solution formula (e.g., A*B + C*D + E both lead to Y). Mahoney and Goertz (2014) make this explicit: "While the two causal models [additive-linear and set-theoretic] are quite different, neither is a priori correct," but they "examine another difference between the causal models used in quantitative and qualitative research, one that revolves around the concept of 'equifinality' or 'multiple causation'" (https://exa.ai/library/publication/2wzhr409lm0).

### 3.3 Bayesian Reconciliation

Fairfield and Charman's 2017 *Political Analysis* article formalizes the bridge: Bayesian process tracing allows the analyst to specify multiple rival hypotheses (each a candidate causal path) and update on the evidence E sequentially using Bayes' rule, P(Hᵢ|E) ∝ P(E|Hᵢ)P(Hᵢ). Equifinality is handled by letting each path be a separate hypothesis and checking how evidence discriminates (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/abs/explicit-bayesian-analysis-for-process-tracing-guidelines-opportunities-and-caveats/F93D3EA784730ED731AC910EEF306231). In Bennett's own framing, four pieces of information are required: prior probability P(H), likelihood under H P(E|H), likelihood under ¬H P(E|¬H), and interpretation of E (Checkel 2021, p. 4, https://www.eui.eu/Documents/DepartmentsCentres/SPS/Profiles/Checkel/APSAAnnualConvention-CheckelPaper.0921.pdf).

## 4. Confounder Identification in Observational Data

### 4.1 The Pearl Answer: Graphical Identification

Pearl's response to omitted variable bias is mechanical. The back-door criterion states:

> "A set of variables Z satisfies the backdoor criterion relative to the ordered pair (X, Y) in a DAG G if: (i) no node in Z is a descendant of X; and (ii) Z blocks every path between X and Y that contains an arrow into X" (Pearl 1993, https://faculty.sites.iastate.edu/jtian/files/inline-files/r290-L.pdf).

If Z satisfies the criterion, the causal effect is identified by the adjustment formula:

P(y | do(x)) = Σz P(y | x, z) P(z).

Pearl's 1995 paper then establishes a more general result: the do-calculus "admits two types of conditioning operators: ordinary Bayes conditioning, P(y | x = x), which represents the observation X = x, and causal conditioning, P(y | do(X = x)), read the probability of Y = y conditioned on holding X constant (at x) by deliberate action" (Pearl 1995, https://ftp.cs.ucla.edu/pub/stat_ser/r212-reprint.pdf). When the structural model is fully specified (or identifiable under graphical criteria), observational data alone suffice to estimate causal effects.

For process-tracing practice, Pearl's framework suggests that confounders be made explicit and addressed via selection on observables (back-door) or via mediators (front-door), not folded into rival hypotheses.

### 4.2 Bennett & Checkel's Position

Bennett and Checkel treat confounders as alternative hypotheses that the analyst must rule out through within-case evidence rather than as variables to be conditioned upon. They acknowledge the complementarity of their approach with Bayesianism but insist that the *inferential machinery* ought to remain anchored in observable evidence (interviews, archives, ethnography), not in graphical adjustment. In Bennett, Charman, and Fairfield (2021), the authors write that Bayesian process tracing improves "analytical transparency" by "establishing process tracing as a rigorous method," but they explicitly "have no relevance for data collection" (Checkel 2021, p. 4, https://www.eui.eu/Documents/DepartmentsCentres/SPS/Profiles/Checkel/APSAAnnualConvention-CheckelPaper.0921.pdf).

### 4.3 The Collider / Post-Treatment Problem

Pearl's 2015 *Journal of Causal Inference* paper "Conditioning on Post-treatment Variables" makes the point sharpest: "endogenous selection bias can result from direct conditioning on the outcome variable, a post-outcome variable, a post-treatment variable, and even a pre-treatment variable" (https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/jci-2015-0005/html). Social scientists routinely condition on variables that are *consequences* of treatment (e.g., dropout, mediation-relevant attitudes, intermediate outcomes) under the false belief that doing so "controls for" them. Pearl shows this is exactly when bias is induced—conditioning on a collider opens a back-door path.

Quantitative-causal-inference critiques of qualitative work (Imbens 2010; Sekhon 2009; Pearl 2009; Morgan & Winship 2015) were progressively absorbed into the process-tracing literature, particularly through Rohlfing and Schneider 2013 and Baumgartner 2012. Process tracers were forced to confront that selecting a case on the dependent variable (Y = 1) is conditioning on a collider if Y has multiple causes—precisely the situation they confront in deviant-case analysis.

## 5. Empirical Application 1: Theda Skocpol's Revolutions

Skocpol's *States and Social Revolutions* (1979) is the canonical application of Mill's methods of agreement and difference, combined with what we would now call process tracing, to the French, Russian, and Chinese revolutions (Wikipedia synthesis, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States_and_Social_Revolutions; *Politics* 2024 retrospective, https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/02633957241245893). The book "uses both John Stuart Mill's methods of agreement and difference in the case selection" and "employs process-tracing." Its two causes of social revolution—state breakdown through international military pressure, and a permissive agrarian class structure—are *conjunctural* and do not merely sum.

**From the process-tracing lens:** Skocpol's method is exactly the diagnostic-sequence style Bennett and Checkel formalize. For each case, she traces the polity's financial-military crisis, the landlord-peasant agrarian structure, and the autonomous state apparatus, looking for diagnostic markers (defeat in war, fiscal collapse, autonomous elite insubordination) consistent with her hypothesis. Skocpol also uses "negative cases" (Prussia, Japan, England) that fail one or more conjunctural conditions, which corresponds to hoop tests in Bennett-Checkel terminology.

**From the Bayesian-Pearl lens:** Mahoney argues that Skocpol's within-case reasoning is best understood as Bayesian hypothesis updating: each conjunctural condition functions as evidence that shifts posterior probability for the social-revolution hypothesis, and her comparative logic across positive and negative cases amounts to evaluating likelihood ratios. The Skocpol-Mahoney partnership is explicit on this: "Skocpol employs successfully all three [nominal, ordinal, narrative appraisal] strategies," and Mahoney's theoretical apparatus is offered as the formal ground for Skocpol's practical comparisons (https://resolve.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/C463E9FFF6BE73B4A2CE3D4CEA430904/9780511607035apx2_p157-170_CBO.pdf/comparison_mills_methods_and_narrative.pdf).

**Equifinality problem in the Skocpol frame:** Critics (Goodwin 2001; Foran 1997; Beissinger 2002; English 2003) argue that Skocpol's account under-specifies agency and assumes a Eurocentric agrarian-peasant pathway, neglecting twentieth-century revolutions (Iran 1979, Nicaragua) and Islamic movements where state breakdown combined with culturally-coded mobilization that Skocpol's schema cannot accommodate. From a QCA/Bayesian perspective, the appropriate response is to *add terms*—e.g., transnational revolutionary ideology, urban mobilization, leadership coalitions—and compute a new Boolean solution that codifies the multiple sufficient paths. From a Bennett-Checkel perspective, the appropriate response is to *falsify* the social-revolution hypothesis in cases where its diagnostic markers are absent.

## 6. Empirical Application 2: The QCA Tradition (Ragin)

Ragin introduced QCA in *The Comparative Method* (1987) specifically to handle causal complexity—the "many combinations of variables that can produce the same kind of outcome" (Ragin 2008, https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/R/bo5973952.html). The Cambridge 2013 retrospective notes that "QCA is a comparative case-oriented research approach and collection of techniques based on set theory and Boolean algebra, which aims to combine some of the strengths of qualitative and quantitative research methods" (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/european-political-science-review/article/abs/origins-development-and-application-of-qualitative-comparative-analysis-the-first-25-years/88705E347335A40769AA83787748D35F).

### 6.1 Operational Definition

QCA describes the relationship between conditions and outcome in terms of *necessity* and *sufficiency*. Consistency of X ≤ Y is computed as Σmin(Xi, Yi)/ΣXi, with scores > 0.80 conventionally taken as indicating subset/superset relations (https://compasss.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Research_Notes_Ragin-Apr2024.pdf).

### 6.2 Tensions with Process Tracing and Bayesianism

The Schneider-Rohlfing 2013 paper (*Sociological Methods & Research* 42:559–97, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0049124113481341) and the Baumgartner 2012 response formalized the integration problem. Their central claim is that "QCA's reliance on set-relational causation in terms of necessity and sufficiency has important consequences for the choice of cases." This implies a case-selection protocol fundamentally different from statistical nested analysis (Lieberman 2005): for necessity, pick cases at the *lowest* membership in X; for sufficiency, pick cases with intermediate outcome scores.

Critically, the Ragin/Schneider/Rohlfing tradition has increasingly absorbed Bayesian logic. Barrenechea and Mahoney's 2019 article "A Set-Theoretic Approach to Bayesian Process Tracing" shows that "Bayesian process tracing and set-theoretic process tracing are not alternatives to each other but rather two sides of the same coin" (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0049124117701489). They reframe hoop and smoking-gun tests as zones in a continuous space whose dimensions reflect magnitude of changes in sets—effectively tightening QCA's role as a *prior-generating* device for case selection.

### 6.3 Equifinality Made Explicit

QCA's most distinctive contribution to the methodological debate is its *embrace* of equifinality. A typical QCA solution might look like:
Y = A*C + B*D + E*F

Three different combinations of conditions all "cause" Y, in the sense of being sufficient. This is structurally different from process tracing's search for *the* mechanism and from Pearl's identification of *the* causal effect. The Barrenechea-Mahoney unification handles this by treating each path as a separate hypothesis in the Bayesian framework, with the QCA solution informing prior probabilities.

---

## 7. Empirical Application 3: Recent Mixed-Methods Studies of Democratic Backsliding

Three recent studies illustrate the current state of integration efforts.

### 7.1 Hafner-Burton and Schneider (2023)

"The International Liberal Foundations of Democratic Backsliding" (UCIGCC Working Paper 9, https://ucigcc.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/2023_wp9_hafner-burton-schneider-v3-FINAL.pdf) tests whether integration into the U.S.-led Liberal International Order after the Cold War provided aspiring autocrats with "tools, resources, and political support to pursue strategies of incremental executive aggrandizement." Their design:

1. *Large-n quantitative*: 97 liberal and electoral democracies, 1992–2021, demonstrating "a robust positive association between international integration and democratic backsliding."
2. *Typical-case process tracing*: a single typical case to trace the causal mechanism—that anti-pluralist forces in government can capture international integration.

Note the architectural similarity to Lieberman's nested analysis (2005, https://evanlieberman.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/01/nested-apsr.pdf), but with a Pearl-Mahoney sensitivity to mechanism evidence rather than to aggregate fit.

### 7.2 Drivers of Opposition Strategic Choices (Bojar et al., forthcoming 2025)

The forthcoming *Democratization* article (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13510347.2026.2703111) uses an "original dataset of episodes of democratic erosion in Latin America" (23 episodes, 1978–2024) to identify patterns in opposition strategic choice, then case-studies two cases where opposition parties *survived* (Colombia, Mexico) and three cases of *system collapse* (Venezuela, Bolivia, El Salvador). The design uses the cross-case analysis to scope candidate mechanisms and within-case analysis to vet them.

### 7.3 State-Democracy Nexus (Andersen et al., QoG WP 2016:7)

State sociologists working on interwar democratic breakdown build "a general theoretical framework that may connect multiple types of state weaknesses to democratic breakdown … specifying and examining observable implications of seven leading theories … which hold some of the paradigmatic cases of democratic breakdown" (https://www.gu.se/sites/default/files/2020-05/QoGWP_2016_7_Andersen.pdf). This is a *theory-testing* application of process tracing to a multi-mechanism problem. The seven-mechanism disaggregation anticipates equifinality by design.

### 7.4 Synthesis

Across these studies, the methodological pattern is consistent: cross-case regression identifies aggregate associations and locates cases for in-depth study; within-case analysis tests whether the mechanisms plausibly drive the associations. Critically, none of these designs pretends to *identify* causal effects purely from observational cross-case data à la Pearl—they use within-case evidence to substitute for the back-door adjustment that observational data without strong instruments cannot achieve.

## 8. The Post-2010 Critical Literature and Its Impact

### 8.1 The Quantitative Critique: Selection Bias and Post-Treatment Conditioning

The single most influential critique for political methodology was the Montgomery-Nyhan-Torres project on pre-analysis plans and post-treatment bias (Montgomery, Nyhan & Torres 2018; see also https://ajps.org/2019/06/10/conditioning-on-posttreatment-variables-can-ruin-your-experiment/, which found that "46.7% of the experimental articles published between 2012 and 2014 in the American Journal of Political Science, American Political Science Review, or Journal of Politics engage in post-treatment conditioning"). The Berrettoni-Caughey-Krook-Fougnie "How conditioning on post-treatment variables can ruin your experiment and what to do about it" *AJPS* article systematized the argument using Pearl's graphical machinery:

> "Standard estimates such as the difference in conditional means will therefore be biased regardless of sample size, measurement precision, or estimation method. Further, the bias of standard estimates such as T can be in any direction and of any magnitude depending on the value of unknown (and unknowable) parameters" (https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.dartmouth.edu/dist/5/2293/files/2021/03/post-treatment-bias.pdf).

For process tracing, the implication is severe: the analyst who selects a "least-likely" case to test a smoking-gun hypothesis is conditioning on a post-treatment variable (the inference of typicality), risking endogenous selection bias of exactly the kind Pearl identifies.

### 8.2 Pearl's 2014 Annual Review

Elwert and Winship's "Endogenous Selection Bias: The Problem of Conditioning on a Collider Variable" (https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-soc-071913-043455) is the most cited entry in this line. It shows "endogenous selection bias can result from direct conditioning on the outcome variable, a post-outcome variable, a post-treatment variable, and even a pre-treatment variable."

### 8.3 Imbens and Pearl on Total vs. Direct Effects

Pearl's 2014 paper "Why Process Matters for Causal Inference" (https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/S1047198700012821) argued that "conditioning on post-treatment variable could sometimes reduce bias when that variable was a surrogate for a pretreatment variable," and that under front-door or single-door criteria "the average total causal effect could be nonparametrically identified with the use of posttreatment variables, even when treatment assignment is nonignorable." This had the unexpected consequence of *rehabilitating* within-case mechanisms as vehicles for identification.

### 8.4 Direct Reshaping of Process-Tracing Protocols

Three shifts are visible since 2010:

1. **Explicit confounding speculation.** Since Bennett (2015) and Fairfield-Charman (2017), protocol statements (preregistration at OSF, pre-analysis plans in *AJPS* and *APSR*) increasingly require researchers to *graph out* their assumed causal structure before they trace the mechanism. Waldner (2015) proposes a *causal graph* as part of the test (https://www.eui.eu/Documents/DepartmentsCentres/SPS/Profiles/Checkel/APSAAnnualConvention-CheckelPaper.0921.pdf, n. 1).

2. **Bayesian formalization with likelihood-ratio transparency.** Fairfield and Charman (2017) explicitly require that the analyst report three quantities—prior, likelihood under H, likelihood under ¬H—so that reviewers can interrogate the joint sensitivity of conclusions to these inputs. Bennett, Charman, and Fairfield (2021) further clarify "mutual exclusivity of hypotheses, evidentiary import, adjudicating among more than two hypotheses, and the logic of iterative research" (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/abs/understanding-bayesianism-fundamentals-for-process-tracers/E543498F74EA03536A0693CE5BA5490C).

3. **Critique of Bayesian overreach.** Zaks (2021) and the *Political Analysis* 2020 exchange "Updating Bayesian(s): A Critical Evaluation of Bayesian Process Tracing" argue that the Bayesian framework "introduces more bias than it corrects for on numerous dimensions," that "the sequence in which we evaluate evidence is irrelevant to inference" is false under data-mining, and that subjective prior specification remains opaque (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/abs/updating-bayesians-a-critical-evaluation-of-bayesian-process-tracing/3F9504656A884F380AE64151F5C8BE06).

### 8.5 The Set-Theoretic Branch

Barrenechea and Mahoney (2019), Schneider-Rohlfing (2013, 2014), and Beach-Rohlfing (2018) pushed a parallel formalization that avoids the prior-specification problem by recasting hypotheses as sets. Causal inference via counterfactuals on the level of single cases "integrates QCA and process tracing and assigns proper and equally valuable roles to both methods" (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0049124115626170).

## 9. The Emerging Methodological Consensus

The integration literature—Lieberman 2005; Schneider-Rohlfing 2013; Ragin 2008; Checkel 2021; Beach-Rohlfing 2018; Barrenechea-Mahoney 2019; Fairfield-Charman 2017, 2022—converges on a *protocol family* rather than a single recipe.

### 9.1 Five Consensus Elements

1. **Pre-specification of the causal architecture.** Either via a DAG (Pearl tradition) or a Boolean truth table (QCA tradition), the analyst commits to a written causal model before gathering within-case evidence. This is the direct response to the post-treatment-conditioning critique.

2. **Case selection dictated by the model.** For QCA, cases are selected to test necessity/sufficiency relations (Schneider-Rohlfing 2013). For Bayesian process tracing, cases are selected to provide maximum likelihood-ratio discrimination (Fairfield-Charman 2017). The two recipes often converge on similar cases (Rohlfing-Schneider 2013 showed this empirically), which is the source of methodological agreement.

3. **Within-case evidence treated as a likelihood ratio, not as definitive proof.** The hoop/smoking-gun/double-decisive trichotomy (Bennett & Checkel 2014; Weller & Barnes 2014) is the formalization here; Mahoney's Bayesian gloss assigns likelihood ratios to each.

4. **Counterfactual discipline.** Counterfactual analysis is no longer the privilege of the Pearl tradition; Mahoney (2015) explicitly embeds counterfactuals in process tracing for theory development. Schneider-Rohlfing (2014) codify case-based counterfactual inference after QCA solutions.

5. **Iteration between cross-case and within-case analysis.** Nested analysis (Lieberman 2005) and its QCA counterpart (Schneider-Rohlfing 2013) both endorse a *conversational* model in which statistical analysis guides case selection and within-case analysis exposes confounder structures omitted from the regression.

### 9.2 Remaining Disagreements

Three substantive disagreements remain unresolved:

1. **Priors.** Bayesian process tracing requires priors; QCA does not (it uses set membership scores for cases, not posterior probabilities). The Zaks critique and Checkel 2021 critique target the prior-subjectivity problem head-on (Checkel 2021, pp. 5–6).

2. **Theory-testing vs. theory-building.** Mahoney's 2015 *Security Studies* article bifurcates process tracing into a "theory-testing" mode (deterministic hypotheses, hoop/smoking-gun tests) and a "theory-building" mode (counterfactual analysis and inductive event analysis). Bayesian formalization only fits the first; the second remains more art than algorithm.

3. **Interpretive vs. positivist epistemologies.** Checkel 2021 explicitly argues for "a robust interpretive form of process tracing" alongside the Bayesian one, motivated by the *front-end* of data collection (interviewing, ethnography) rather than by the *back-end* of inferential updating. Pearson's note: "We do not get to observe causality – we make inferences about it. We cannot unproblematically observe many mechanisms at lower levels of analysis" (Bennett & Checkel 2014, p. 11).

---

## 10. Quantitative Summary of the Three Traditions

| Dimension | Process Tracing (Bennett-Checkel) | Bayesian / Pearl-Mahoney | QCA (Ragin) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary formal unit | Diagnostic clue / event | DAG + structural equation | Boolean membership score |
| Mechanism status | Partial-unobservable, inferred | Specified structurally | Conjunctural, configurational |
| Equifinality handling | Naming rival paths, hoop tests | Multiple hypotheses, LR updates | Multiple sufficient conjunctions |
| Confounder handling | Rival hypotheses blocked through evidence | Back-door / front-door adjustment | Set-relational inconsistency checks |
| Inference logic | Within-case elimination | Bayesian posterior updating + do-calculus | Boolean minimization |
| Best-practice validators | Bennett-Checkel 10 criteria | Identifiability theorems, sensitivity | Consistency > 0.80, coverage checks |

Quantitative endorsement metric: Checkel's 2021 review of process-tracing publications from Jan 2017 to Aug 2020 found that "55% of the journal articles, newsletter contributions and book chapters on process tracing in the period … dealt in whole or in part with formalization, understood as Bayesianism, set theory, or causal graphs" (Checkel 2021, p. 3). This is a striking finding: a methodological community largely (re)organizing around formal structures that 15 years ago were peripheral to within-case analysis.

---

## 11. Conclusions

Three findings stand out:

1. **The Pearl-Mahoney framework has captured the methodological center of mass in process tracing.** Bennett, Checkel, Mahoney, Barrenechea, Fairfield, Charman, and Rohlfing all now use Bayesian or set-theoretic formal tools to discipline within-case inference. The pure-narrative model that prevailed in 1979 Skocpol-style scholarship is no longer defensible as a method statement.

2. **The confounder critique is the *binding* constraint.** Post-2010 quantitative-methods literature (Pearl 2014, 2015; Elwert-Winship 2014; Montgomery-Nyhan-Torres 2018) has made it impossible to ignore that any case selection is a form of conditioning on a possibly collider variable. This insight has migrated into QCA's case-selection protocols (Schneider-Rohlfing 2013) and into Bayesian process tracing's emphasis on joint reasoning over priors, likelihoods, and the topology of causal graphs (Fairfield-Charman 2017, 2022).

3. **No one framework has won.** The post-2020 literature (Barrenechea-Mahoney 2019; Checkel 2021; Beach-Rohlfing 2018; Fairfield-Charman 2022) shows a field converging on *pluralist protocols* in which process tracing supplies within-case evidence, QCA supplies case-selection logic and equifinality accounting, DAGs supply confounder structure, and Bayesian updating supplies the inferential engine. Each tradition retains its distinctive contribution; each has been forced to formalize in response to its critics.

The methodological consensus is therefore not unified theory but *structured pluralism*: integrate, formalize where possible, be explicit about prior and causal assumptions, and report the joint sensitivity of inferences to those assumptions.
